- After 48–72 hours, new organ failure, persistent systemic inflammation or inability to feed changes the problem.
- CT/MRI may be used selectively for complications, while suspected biliary cholangitis or persistent duct obstruction prompts GI/ERCP discussion.
- At one to several weeks, infected necrosis, gastric outlet obstruction, fistula and delayed haemorrhage can dominate. A sudden deterioration after initial improvement warrants assessment for infected necrosis, bleeding pseudoaneurysm, abdominal compartment syndrome, venous thrombosis and organ failure.

items.title: 17. ICU management: ischaemic, perforated and obstructed gut
items.priority: P2 HIGH (1 parent LO) + P5 MINIMUM (1 parent LO)
items.body:
### 17.1 Acute mesenteric ischaemia is an early recognition problem

- Forms include embolic occlusion (e.g., AF), atherosclerotic SMA thrombosis, nonocclusive mesenteric ischaemia (low flow/high vasopressors/shock) and mesenteric venous thrombosis.
- A patient may initially have severe **pain out of proportion** to examination; later peritonism, GI bleeding, acidosis, rising lactate, organ failure and shock imply irreversible or advanced injury.
- A normal initial lactate or soft abdomen **does not exclude** mesenteric ischaemia.
- Obtain urgent contrast-enhanced CTA to identify vessels and bowel injury; do not automatically withhold life-saving imaging for moderate renal dysfunction, and do not delay source control in an unstable patient with peritonitis.
- Provide analgesia, broad-spectrum antibiotics when transmural injury/sepsis is suspected, correct hypovolaemia and support organ perfusion.
- Therapeutic anticoagulation is considered for arterial/venous thrombotic disease after bleeding/surgical assessment.
- Prompt multidisciplinary revascularisation (endovascular/open) is central in salvageable arterial ischaemia; peritonitis/necrotic bowel requires urgent resection.
- A second-look operation at ≈24–48 h may be planned when bowel viability is uncertain, because the surgeon’s judgement of viability can change over hours after reperfusion or shock [R15].

**Mesenteric circulation explained:**

- The superior mesenteric artery supplies most small bowel and right colon; intestinal mucosa has high oxygen demand, making it especially vulnerable when arterial inflow or systemic perfusion fails.
- An embolus from AF may abruptly occlude the SMA; atherosclerotic thrombosis often occurs on pre-existing ostial disease, sometimes after a history of postprandial pain and weight loss.
- Mesenteric venous thrombosis blocks drainage, producing congestion and oedema before arterial inflow may fail.
- Nonocclusive mesenteric ischaemia occurs in low-flow or intense vasoconstrictive states without an occluding clot.
- Initially painful ischaemia may have a soft abdomen because the visceral mucosa is affected before the parietal peritoneum; later transmural necrosis produces peritonitis, bacterial translocation and shock.
- After restoring flow, reperfusion may release potassium, acid and inflammatory mediators.

**Nonocclusive mesenteric ischaemia:**

- Think after cardiac surgery, profound shock, high-dose catecholamines or severe HF.
- Reduce harmful vasoconstriction when possible, restore cardiac output, identify sepsis and optimise perfusion.
- A sedated, pressor-dependent ICU patient may have non-occlusive low-flow ischaemia with little pain.
- This is not a rationale to stop all pressors in a critically hypotensive patient; adequate MAP/organ flow remains necessary.
- Clinical deterioration after ‘successful’ revascularisation can reflect microvascular injury, reperfusion, oedema or residual dead bowel.

### 17.2 Perforated or obstructed bowel: organ support must accompany source control

- Perforation leads to bacterial/chemical peritonitis, sepsis, vasoplegia, ileus and profound third-space losses.
- Control contamination (surgery/IR), antibiotics, haemodynamic and respiratory support and monitored nutrition; if the bowel is grossly oedematous or physiology deranged, temporary abdominal closure and planned relook may be safer.
- Obstruction causes vomiting/aspiration risk, fluid and chloride loss, distension, reduced FRC, and may progress to strangulation; replace deficits, decompress appropriately and monitor for ischaemia.
- Assess intra-abdominal pressure in tense or distended patients with rising ventilatory or renal problems (see 17.4).

**Reperfusion after bowel surgery:**

- Unresolved tachycardia, escalating vasopressors, new oliguria, persistent acidosis, abdominal distension, raised gastric residuals or GI bleeding warrant reevaluation for residual ischaemia, leak or compartment syndrome.
- Additional postoperative anticoagulation may be necessary after mesenteric vascular intervention, balanced against haemostasis and neuraxial-catheter safety.

- **Postoperative ileus** can mimic obstruction/leak; assess surgery, NG output, imaging and systemic illness before ‘treating ileus’ with prokinetics or feeding.

### 17.3 Open abdomen and ongoing deterioration

- An open abdomen requires a written plan for fluid/protein losses, visceral protection, temperature, sedoanalgesia, nutrition, abdominal pressure and re-exploration.
- Trend abdominal examination, stoma appearance/output, lactate/blood gas, drains, renal and respiratory function, but interpret each as imperfect; persistent deterioration warrants repeat anatomical investigation and source-control discussion.

### 17.4 Abdominal compartment syndrome

- Fluid accumulation, bowel oedema, ascites, haemorrhage or tight abdominal closure increase intra-abdominal pressure (IAP).
- High IAP elevates the diaphragm and intrathoracic pressure, causing poor respiratory compliance; compresses renal veins and kidneys, causing oliguria; reduces venous return and splanchnic perfusion, worsening shock and bowel ischaemia.
- ACS means sustained IAP >20 mmHg with NEW organ dysfunction, rather than any distended abdomen alone.
- Serial bladder-pressure measurement in standardised conditions is useful when clinically suspected.
- Sedation/analgesia, gastric/rectal decompression, judicious fluid strategy, drainage of collections and ultimately decompressive laparotomy may be needed. [WSACS definitions]
- If there is **worsening abdominal distension with high airway pressure, reduced urine output and shock**, measure intra-abdominal pressure and call the surgeons. ACS can develop after massive resuscitation, pancreatitis, peritonitis or tight closure.

items.title: 18. ICU care after major abdominal surgery
items.body:
### 18.1 Priorities on ICU admission: what changes compared with ordinary PACU?

- Obtain a **surgical and physiological handover:** pathology and source control, anastomoses/stoma/organ remnant, ischaemia or clamp duration, ongoing bleeding/contamination, planned second look, antibiotic plan, fluid/blood/products, analgesic catheters, antithrombotics, oxygenation/ventilation and explicit triggers for urgent reoperation.
- Operative success must be assessed with organ function, not just stable BP at theatre exit.
- High-risk patients may require invasive monitoring, serial ABG/lactate, Hb/fibrinogen, coagulation, K/Ca/Mg, glucose, renal function, temperature, perfusion and drain/stoma output.

**Haemodynamics:**

- Differentiate persistent haemorrhage, distributive shock, cardiac dysfunction and intra-abdominal pressure; treat each mechanism.
- Use balanced fluid and dynamic perfusion reassessment while avoiding fluid accumulation that worsens lung, bowel and wound oedema.
- Reduce fluid once resuscitation is no longer needed, replace ongoing NG/stoma losses explicitly and reassess daily weight/balance.
- Vasopressors can support perfusion but may worsen gut ischaemia when excessive; target adequate flow and a sensible MAP based on patient and disease.
- Rising lactate may reflect hepatic clearance impairment, continued ischaemia, beta-agonists or ongoing sepsis—investigate the trend.

**Respiratory:**

- Early extubation can support mobilisation but is unsafe with ongoing shock, significant pulmonary oedema, acidosis, poor cough, severe aspiration or major thoracic components.
- Lung-protective ventilation and judicious sedation prevent secondary harm.
- Prior oesophagectomy, recurrent-laryngeal injury or abdominal distension complicates aspiration and ventilation.
- Use multimodal, respiratory-preserving analgesia, but monitor sedatives/opioids and catheter-related hypotension.
- Distinguish postoperative atelectasis, pneumonia, ARDS, pulmonary embolism and fluid overload when new hypoxaemia appears.

**Sepsis/source control:**

- Ensure antimicrobial timing/duration, cultures and stewardship.
- Reevaluate daily: an unexplained new vasopressor requirement, fever, delirium, leukocytosis/CRP rise, wound/drain changes, new bile or feculent material and persistent ileus can signal leak/collection.
- CT or IR drainage and return to theatre should not be delayed by endless antibiotic broadening.
- Preserve anastomotic perfusion, prevent hypothermia, manage glycaemia, encourage early enteral nutrition when safe and provide VTE prophylaxis after haemostasis and catheter review.
- Plan for delirium prevention, mobilisation, nutrition, psychosocial recovery and critical-care follow-up.

### 18.2 Procedure-specific ‘do not miss’ complications

- A detailed handover should state what anatomy was constructed, which structures were at risk, the location of drains/stomas and which findings require urgent imaging or return to theatre.

- **Oesophagectomy:** conduit ischaemia/leak, pneumonia/ARDS, atrial fibrillation, chylothorax and vocal-cord dysfunction; critical early changes include new tachycardia, pleural collection or unexpected drain output. New severe pain in a patient with an epidural must not be assumed to be inadequate local anaesthetic.
- **Pancreatectomy:** pancreatic fistula, delayed haemorrhage/pseudoaneurysm, delayed gastric emptying, abscess, hypoglycaemia/hyperglycaemia and sepsis. Any sentinel bleed is urgent.
- **Liver resection:** bleeding, bile leak, post-hepatectomy liver failure, hypoglycaemia, AKI, new coagulopathy and impaired lactate clearance.
- **Colorectal resection:** anastomotic leak, bowel ischaemia, prolonged ileus versus obstruction, stoma losses, VTE and pelvic infection.
- **Emergency bowel/liver trauma:** missed necrotic bowel or bleeding, compartment syndrome, open-abdomen losses, planned relook and ongoing shock.
- **Bariatric/reconstruction:** gastric staple-line leak, internal hernia, VTE, opioid-induced ventilatory impairment with OSA/OHS, flap thrombosis and pressure injury; an acute flap colour or Doppler change is a time-critical vessel problem, so call the surgeon immediately.

### 18.3 Nutrition, functional recovery and safe discharge

- Remove unnecessary vascular and urinary catheters, plan stoma education and mobilisation, review anticoagulation, analgesic route and opioid taper.
- ICU discharge is not safe merely because vasopressors have stopped if a leak or wound complication is evolving.

**ICU nutrition after upper-GI and bowel surgery**

**Assess on admission:**

- Review weight change, pre-existing malnutrition/sarcopenia, recent oral intake, pancreatic insufficiency, expected bowel continuity and whether feeding access was placed.
- A “normal BMI” does not exclude malnutrition.
- Decide if the patient can safely eat, whether the gut is perfused and functioning, and whether jejunal or gastric feeding is safer for the reconstruction.
- Active shock with escalating vasopressors, suspected bowel ischaemia or uncontrolled obstruction calls for stabilisation and reassessment, not blindly advancing enteral feed.
- The 2025 ESPEN surgical nutrition update emphasises early feeding where feasible and early identification of nutrition risk, particularly in major upper-GI surgery [R21].

**Choose route and dose:**

- Prefer oral/enteral support when feasible, including NG/NJ or surgical jejunostomy in selected patients; parenteral nutrition is appropriate when the bowel cannot provide sufficient intake (e.g. persistent obstruction, high-output proximal fistula, severe intolerance).
- In critical illness, energy targets are uncertain early; avoid overfeeding, especially during the acute hypermetabolic phase, and individualise protein with dietetics (commonly around 1.2–2.0 g/kg/day, with adjustments for body size, kidney function and clinical phase).
- Monitor actual intake rather than merely what is prescribed.
- Feeding routes after oesophagectomy or Whipple must follow operative instructions to protect new joins.

**Monitor tolerance and refeeding:**

- Track abdominal exam, distension, new pain, stool/stoma output, gastric aspirates in context, glucose, sodium, phosphate, magnesium, potassium, fluid balance and haemodynamic response.
- A fixed 200 mL gastric-aspirate threshold is not a universally accepted contemporary stop rule; act on clinical intolerance and current local ICU nutrition policy.
- If high refeeding risk, give thiamine and low initial energy with regular replacement of phosphate/K/Mg.
- Avoid long unreviewed “NPO” orders after surgery; likewise do not continue feeds through a suspected ischaemic bowel.

### 18.4 A structured ICU problem list after GI surgery

**Day 0:**

- Record the operation’s actual anatomy, resuscitation, airway/ventilator and analgesic strategy, drain outputs and postoperative surgical escalation triggers.
- **Days 1–3:** review fluid accumulation, early AKI, respiratory complications, bleeding, infection, VTE prevention and early nutrition; recheck whether IV maintenance and oxygen remain necessary.
- **Days 3–7:** increasing vigilance for anastomotic leak, pancreatic fistula/sentinel haemorrhage, abscess, delayed bowel ischaemia and liver dysfunction.
- These are illustrative time patterns, not rules that exclude earlier/later complications.
- An ICU plan for an open abdomen must state relook timing, organ support, nutrition and losses.
- Every day ask whether worsening physiology reflects a new surgical problem rather than merely inadequate ICU medication.

### 18.5 Postoperative complications: a diagnosis-driven escalation framework

- A day-1 tachycardic patient after major bowel surgery: examine pain, temperature, drains and stoma, fluid balance, blood loss, oxygenation and ECG; distinguish hypovolaemia/bleeding, pulmonary embolism, evolving sepsis, myocardial injury and postoperative pain.
- Transfuse based on clinical bleeding/oxygen delivery rather than an isolated number.
- A falling Hb with new abdominal distension warrants haemorrhage investigation; low urine output alone is not an indication for repeated 1-L crystalloid challenges.
- At day 3–7, new persistent tachycardia, fever, pain, ileus, confusion or vasopressor need may represent an anastomotic leak or collection; do not wait for obvious faeculent drain output.
- Discuss urgent CT with appropriate contrast and possible drainage or reoperation with the surgical team, while giving antibiotics/resuscitation when clinically indicated.

**Discharge from ICU must include an explicit contingency plan:**

- What change in HR, oxygen requirement, lactate, abdominal signs, drain character or stoma output prompts an immediate call.
- Who may restart anticoagulants.
- How the epidural/peripheral catheter will be removed safely.
- How oral/enteral feeding and analgesia will progress.
- Who owns the imaging/reoperation decision, and whether a surgeon is immediately contactable overnight. Include the number and type of anastomoses, drain and stoma plans, antibiotic stop or review date, mobility goals and delirium risk; general postoperative guidelines cannot replace the surgeon’s reintervention thresholds and the patient’s goals.

**Epidural and PCA safety after complex surgery**

**Daily epidural review:**

- Document catheter level/skin depth, intended dermatomal coverage, actual sensory and motor block, local anaesthetic/opioid solution, pain at rest and movement, sedation, respiratory rate, hypotension and motor weakness.
- An abruptly dense motor block, severe new back pain, sensory level change or new bladder/bowel dysfunction demands immediate cessation of the infusion, neurological examination and urgent senior investigation for an epidural haematoma/abscess; timely MRI and decompression are time-critical.
- A rising block may cause extensive sympathetic blockade, respiratory compromise or bradycardia.
- Do not treat all hypotension simply with fluid if the cause is neuraxial sympathectomy.

**Anticoagulants and removal:**

- Both placement AND catheter removal are neuraxial procedures.
- Full-dose anticoagulants, prophylactic LMWH, DOACs, renal impairment and changing coagulation after liver surgery each demand drug/dose-specific timing.
- The 2025 ASRA fifth-edition guidance differentiates low- from high-dose anticoagulation; never use fixed intervals without checking the actual agent, last dose, renal function, procedure urgency and local policy.
- Document a plan for VTE prevention before placing the epidural and before removing it.

**PCA safety and transition:**

- A PCA requires a patient sufficiently awake to operate it; relatives must never press the button for them.
- Avoid routine basal opioid infusions in opioid-naïve/high-risk OSA/OHS patients without specialist oversight, since sedation and ventilatory impairment can be concealed by oxygen supplementation.
- Provide a bridge to enteral or subcutaneous analgesia before stopping epidural/PCA and verify the functioning GI route; absorption may be impaired after major resection or with ileus. [ASRA 2025]

items.title: 19. Organ procurement after neurological determination of death
items.body:
### 19.1 Ethical, physiological and procedural foundations

- This chapter covers **anaesthetic care for organ procurement in a donor declared dead by neurological criteria** (donation after neurological determination of death, DBD).
- Do not confuse this with donation after circulatory determination of death (DCD), which has a distinct legal and ethical pathway: withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment, observation after circulatory arrest, independent declaration of death, a mandatory stand-off period prescribed by local legislation, and warm-ischaemia timing.
- Before theatre confirm that death has been determined and documented by authorised clinicians under current legislation and ANZICS/local protocols, that donation authorisation and organ allocation are completed, and that the procurement team’s plan is understood.
- Anaesthetic involvement is **physiological donor support**, prevention of spinal reflex movement (if requested), ventilatory management and teamwork; it is not administering anaesthesia to a living conscious patient.
- Maintain respect for the deceased, privacy and family wishes, with clear communication among retrieval, donor ICU, theatre and family-support staff, and document handover to mortuary/family teams.
- The current ANZICS Statement on Death and Organ Donation is the appropriate A/NZ governance source [R16].

**DBD physiology and theatre sequence for a first-time retrieval:**

- After certified neurological death, the patient can retain a beating heart and perfused organs through mechanical ventilation and cardiovascular support despite irreversible loss of brain function.
- The anaesthetist may receive a donor already intubated and on vasopressors, then connect theatre monitors/ventilator and continue physiological support while abdominal/thoracic teams surgically expose and cannulate great vessels.
- The surgeon often gives systemic heparin before aortic cross-clamping when prescribed, cannulates for cold preservative perfusion and clamps the aorta to start organ cooling.
- At that point graft perfusion is provided by preservation solution rather than the donor circulation, and blood-pressure support usually ceases as directed.
- This sequence differs fundamentally from organ transplantation into a living recipient: the aim in the donor is preserving organ quality, avoiding preventable instability and maintaining respectful, legally authorised care throughout.
- Use the current Organ Donation New Zealand forms (updated October 2026) rather than an old downloaded template; the anaesthetist does not independently establish death or donation authorisation [R16, R22].

**Brain-death physiology:**

- After a sympathetic ‘catecholamine storm’, loss of sympathetic tone can cause vasoplegia and low SVR; myocardial stunning may coexist.
- Diabetes insipidus from hypothalamic–pituitary injury causes polyuria, hypernatraemia and intravascular depletion.
- Poikilothermia, altered thyroid/adrenal axes, glycaemic disturbance and lung injury (neurogenic pulmonary oedema, aspiration, pneumonia) threaten graft quality.
- Organ-specific goals for oxygenation, cardiac output, preload, sodium/glucose, Hb and temperature are agreed with the donor ICU/transplant teams; fixed universal thresholds should not be invented.
- The preferred response to hypotension depends on vasoplegia versus true volume depletion versus poor cardiac function.
- Treat excessive urine output with rising sodium as possible diabetes insipidus: measure urine and plasma osmolality and replace free-water losses with fluid and desmopressin/vasopressin per donor protocol, monitoring sodium correction safely and avoiding rapid change without input from donation staff.
- Maintain temperature and prevent lung injury.

### 19.2 Theatre checklist and care before aortic cross-clamp

- Confirm identity/authorisations and organ list, expected sequence, airway/ventilator/vasopressors, vascular access, laboratory results (blood group, organ function, electrolytes, ABG), antibiotics and cultures transferred, and planned heparin. Clarify whether heart and lungs are being retrieved before accepting manoeuvres that threaten their function.
- Maintain lung-protective ventilation and PEEP as feasible for lung procurement, avoid oxygen toxicity where possible while preserving adequate gas exchange, and communicate with retrieval surgeons if lungs are being recovered.
- Continue donor haemodynamic optimisation, check ionised Ca/K/Na/glucose, warming, perfusion and fluid balance.
- Large shifts can occur during dissection, sternotomy/laparotomy or venous manipulation; an arterial line and vasoactive infusions are usually useful, and major blood loss or sudden hypotension before cross-clamp may compromise organ viability, so coordinate with the surgeons.
- Spinal-mediated movements or haemodynamic responses may persist after brain death, and **neuromuscular blockade can be administered to prevent movement** in coordination with the retrieval team.
- Such reflexes do not establish consciousness.
- Some centres administer volatile agents for haemodynamic manipulation or immobility, but a conventional anaesthetic depth is not required for unconsciousness in a correctly declared DBD donor; follow donor procurement standards rather than a generic GA recipe.

- The surgeon may request systemic heparin and organ-specific perfusion preparation.
- Confirm timing of aortic cross-clamp, cold preservation solution and flush; coordinate with cardiac/lung, liver, renal and other teams.
- At cross-clamp and cessation of circulation, document time accurately; physiological support is discontinued when agreed.
- Avoid unnecessary delays that increase organ warm ischaemia.
- After retrieval, ensure respectful body care and clear documentation.

### 19.3 Donor-specific rescue: hypotension, polyuria, poor oxygenation

- If a DBD donor develops **hypotension**, re-evaluate actual circulating volume, haemorrhage/insufflation or surgical compression, vasoplegia and myocardial dysfunction.
- Give targeted fluid only if hypovolaemic/responsive and tolerating, otherwise use titrated vasopressors/inotropes.
- Persistent low output threatens kidneys/liver/heart even if MAP is restored by high SVR.
- With **hypoxaemia**, assess tube position, suction, recruit atelectasis judiciously and use lung-protective ventilation and oxygenation targets consistent with lung procurement.
- Notify the retrieval teams if an organ becomes unsuitable or perfusion deteriorates.

items.title: 20. Worked integration: the six decisions that separate an excellent answer from a generic list
items.los: Integrates the outcomes in this set
items.body:
### Case A — Unstable small-bowel obstruction with aspiration risk

- A 79-year-old with several days of vomiting, no stool, distension, K 2.7 mmol/L, bicarbonate 36 mmol/L, creatinine rising and BP 96/58 needs laparotomy for closed-loop obstruction.
- **Preoperative:** confirm suspected strangulation on CTA and whether source control is immediate; assess perfusion and ECG, place IVs, group/crossmatch and initiate guided chloride/potassium/fluid replacement.
- Correct dangerous hypokalaemia sufficiently for safer induction when time allows, but do not delay threatened bowel indefinitely; monitor Mg and repeat sampling.
- High aspirate volume despite fasting requires NGT decompression if safe and RSI with ETT, suction, preoxygenation and vasopressor plan.
- **Intraoperative:** monitor haemodynamics, perfusion, blood loss and bowel viability; distinguish simple adhesiolysis from necrotic bowel requiring resection/stoma.
- Ventilation may improve after decompression.
- **Postoperative:** replace measured NGT/stoma losses, correct ongoing electrolytes, watch for mesenteric ischaemia and infection; feed when anatomy and gut recovery permit.
- Do not overinterpret the metabolic alkalosis as a benign finding in the face of a strangulated bowel.

### Case B — Upper-GI bleeding with liver disease, sedation requested

- A cirrhotic patient is vomiting fresh blood with new encephalopathy and persistent hypotension.
- **Diagnosis:** likely variceal bleeding but ulcer and other sources remain possible.
- **Immediate care:** blood-based resuscitation, calcium/warming, vasoactive portal therapy plus antibiotics, airway and perfusion assessment and urgent endoscopist/ICU/IR coordination.
- **Airway:** active haematemesis and confusion favour cuffed intubation after preparing for a cardiovascular crash; deep sedation with an unprotected airway is unsafe.
- **Endoscopic management:** plan banding, secondary rescue if uncontrolled; distinguish restrictive stable transfusion from massive ongoing bleeding.
- **Post:** rebleeding, infection/aspiration, renal injury and encephalopathy.
- This is not a case in which a ‘routine gastroscopy propofol bolus’ addresses the risks.

### Case C — Prolonged robotic pelvic surgery with worsening physiology

- A patient in steep head-down tilt develops plateau pressure 34 cmH₂O, EtCO₂ 57 mmHg, facial oedema and MAP 58 during pneumoperitoneum.
- **Analyse:** elevated abdominal and intrathoracic pressure reduce compliance and venous return, while CO₂ absorption increases ventilatory demand.
- **Act:** communicate with surgeon to lower insufflation pressure/lessen tilt if feasible; verify ETT position, oxygenation, pneumothorax, subcutaneous gas and cardiac output; adjust minute ventilation safely and support perfusion according to cause.
- Review cumulative fluid/venous congestion and whether continuing the robotic position is safe.
- Before extubation assess airway oedema and respiratory reserve; prolonged head-down oedema means normal SpO₂ on ventilator is not adequate assurance.

### Case D — Partial hepatectomy with major venous bleeding

- During liver transection at requested low CVP, major bleeding begins and MAP falls.
- **Ask whether inflow is controlled:** Pringle manoeuvre controls portal venous/hepatic arterial inflow but not hepatic venous/IVC back-bleeding.
- Communicate immediately, support cardiac output and perfusion with blood-based resuscitation and targeted vasopressor, use calcium/warming and haemostatic monitoring, do not cling to CVP <5 during exsanguination.
- Recognise risk of gas embolism through open veins and monitor sudden ETCO₂/oxygenation change.
- After bleeding control, transition to measured fluid restoration and monitor postoperative hypoglycaemia, liver function, bile leak and coagulopathy.

### Case E — Post-Whipple ‘sentinel bleed’ with tachycardia

- On day 6, drain blood changes from serous to red, Hb falls modestly and pulse is 115 despite a tolerable BP.
- Do not assume a small drain volume excludes major injury.
- Obtain immediate senior HPB/IR/ICU input, resuscitate, crossmatch, monitor serial Hb/coags/lactate, arrange urgent CTA/angiography or surgical control according to physiology.
- Avoid delaying with routine ward observation.
- Review anticoagulants and pain catheters.
- After control, monitor pancreatoenteric fistula, biliary sepsis, glucose and nutrition.

### Case F — Pancreatitis fluids cause respiratory deterioration

- A patient with alcohol-related pancreatitis receives repeated boluses because lipase remains high; after 24 h they have worsening hypoxia, bilateral crepitations and rising abdominal pressure despite MAP 75. **Reassess the hypothesis:** high lipase is not a volume target, and apparent pancreatic inflammation does not justify indefinite aggressive fluids.
- Examine haemodynamic responsiveness and congestion, repeat gas/renal function and fluid balance, assess for ARDS, fluid overload, cardiogenic cause or abdominal compartment physiology.
- Reduce unnecessary fluids, support ventilation and consider organ-support/diuresis when appropriate.

items.title: Landmark trials at a glance
items.body:
- **T1.** [RELIEF — Restrictive versus Liberal Fluid Therapy for Major Abdominal Surgery (Myles et al., NEJM 2018)](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1801601). Population: approximately 3000 higher-risk patients undergoing major elective abdominal surgery, with perioperative restrictive versus more liberal IV fluid policies. Main finding: no significant improvement in one-year disability-free survival with restriction (81.9% versus 82.3%); **AKI was greater with the restrictive strategy (8.6% versus 5.0%)**. Application: avoid dogmatic zero-balance fluid treatment and protect renal/organ perfusion, while also avoiding overload. Limitations: studied planned major abdominal surgery in higher-risk patients, not uncontrolled haemorrhage, emergency septic laparotomy or liver resection; ‘liberal’ is not carte blanche for excessive fluids.

- **T2.** [OPTIMISE II — Cardiac output-guided haemodynamic therapy during major GI surgery (BMJ 2024)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39626899/). Population: 2498 older patients having major elective gastrointestinal surgery, assigned routine cardiac-output-guided IV fluid plus low-dose inotrope versus usual care. Main finding: no reduction in postoperative infection (23.2% versus 22.7%); early cardiac events/tachyarrhythmias were increased in the intervention group. Application: haemodynamic monitors may help selected high-risk patients, but a rigid monitor-plus-inotrope strategy is **not automatically superior**. Limitations: specific protocol and predominantly older elective patients; does not imply flow measurement is useless for every patient with shock or complex surgery.

- **T3.** [Villanueva et al. — Restrictive versus liberal transfusion in acute upper-GI bleeding (NEJM 2013)](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1211801). Population: acute upper-GI bleeding, restrictive Hb threshold around 70 g/L versus liberal around 90 g/L after assessment/resuscitation. Main finding: restrictive transfusion improved clinical outcomes, including survival/rebleeding in the studied population. Application: do not overtransfuse a stabilised UGIB patient, especially with portal-hypertension risks. Limitations: a trial policy is **not** a fixed trigger during uncontrolled exsanguination, and cardiac ischaemia or other patient-specific conditions may require individual thresholds.

- **T4.** [WATERFALL — Aggressive or Moderate Fluid Resuscitation in Acute Pancreatitis (NEJM 2022)](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2202884). Population: 249 patients in the interim analysis with acute pancreatitis randomised to aggressive or moderate lactated-Ringer’s regimens; stopped early for safety. Main finding: **fluid overload 20.5% versus 6.3%** with aggressive fluids, with no significant reduction in moderately severe/severe pancreatitis. Application: use moderated, repeated fluid reassessment rather than automatic large infusions. Limitations: excluded some very severe/advanced organ-failure presentations; a profoundly hypovolaemic or shocked patient still needs individualised resuscitation.

- **T5.** [HALT-IT — Tranexamic acid in significant gastrointestinal bleeding (Lancet 2020)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32563378/). Population: around 12,000 adults with significant upper or lower GI bleeding randomised to high-dose TXA or placebo. Main finding: bleeding death at five days was unchanged (~4% in both groups); increased venous thromboembolism (0.8% versus 0.4%) and seizures. Application: **do not give routine TXA** for non-traumatic GI haemorrhage on the assumption that trauma results generalise. Limitations: evaluates a particular high-dose, prolonged regimen in GI bleeding; does not disprove TXA benefit in unrelated indications such as selected trauma or surgical bleeding.

- **T6.** [PANTER — Step-up approach versus open necrosectomy for necrotising pancreatitis (NEJM 2010)](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa0908821). Population: infected necrotising pancreatitis, minimally invasive drainage-first with escalation versus primary open necrosectomy. Main finding: step-up strategy reduced major complications or death composite compared with routine open operation, while not powered to prove a mortality difference alone. Application: consider delayed multidisciplinary drainage/debridement after stabilisation rather than immediate open necrosectomy for every necrotic collection. Limitations: selected patients and available expertise; uncontrolled sepsis or compartment syndrome can necessitate earlier intervention.

- **T7.** [PONCHO — Same-admission versus interval cholecystectomy after mild gallstone pancreatitis (Lancet 2015)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26460661/). Population: patients recovering from mild gallstone pancreatitis. Main finding: same-admission surgery reduced recurrent gallstone-related events/readmission compared with delayed surgery. Application: plan index-admission cholecystectomy when clinically suitable once mild pancreatitis settles, rather than routinely deferring. Limitations: does not mean immediate cholecystectomy is safe during severe pancreatitis, persistent organ failure, infected collections or high surgical risk.

items.title: Reading list and linked references
items.body:
## Linked references and source register

Contemporary guidance is preferred for recommendation thresholds; older BJA Education reviews remain valuable for physiology and procedural thinking.

**Curriculum and general surgery resources**

- **R1.** [ANZCA Anaesthesia Training Program Curriculum — official trainee toolkit](https://www.anzca.edu.au/education-and-training/anaesthesia-training-and-pathways/anaesthesia-training-program/anaesthesia-trainee-toolkit). Source of curriculum and official examination-learning-outcome framework.
- **R2.** [ERAS Society: Emergency laparotomy, Part 1 — preoperative identification, rapid assessment and optimisation (2021)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8026421/). Best for simultaneous resuscitation, source-control urgency, analgesia, consent and risk appraisal.
- **R3.** [ERAS Society: Emergency laparotomy, Part 2 — intraoperative and postoperative care (2023)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10241558/). Best for surgery-specific physiologic support, nutrition, fluid therapy and ICU recovery.
- **R4.** [ERAS Society: Elective colorectal surgery guideline (2025)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40783294/). Current perioperative bowel-fluid, analgesia, drains, nutrition and mobilisation recommendations. Read its population limits before applying to sepsis or perforation.

**Gastrointestinal haemorrhage, endoscopy and hepatobiliary diseases**

- **R5.** [ESGE: Endoscopic diagnosis/management of peptic ulcer bleeding, 2026 update](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42127996/). Current nonvariceal bleeding/endoscopy timing, high-risk ulcer techniques, recurrent bleeding and transcatheter embolisation guidance.
- **R6.** [British Society of Gastroenterology: Sedation in gastrointestinal endoscopy guideline (2023/24)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10850688/). Airway and ventilatory monitoring, high-risk procedural sedation and advanced endoscopy.
- **R7.** [Baveno VII: Renewing consensus in portal hypertension (2022)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11090185/). Cirrhosis/variceal haemorrhage: targeted resuscitation, vasoactive therapy, antibiotics, early endoscopic and TIPS strategies.
- **R8.** [BJA Education: Anaesthesia for minimally invasive abdominal and pelvic surgery (Carey, Jones & Fawcett, 2019)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7807985/). Core physiology of CO₂ pneumoperitoneum, body positioning, perfusion, ventilation and patient access.
- **R9.** [ACG Guideline: Management of Acute Pancreatitis (2024)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38857482/). Diagnostic criteria, severity, CT timing, feeding, fluid resuscitation, antibiotics and biliary intervention.

**Complex procedures and ICU**

- **R10.** [ERAS Society: Guidelines for perioperative care in oesophagectomy](https://erassociety.org/guideline/guidelines-for-perioperative-care-in-esophagectomy-enhanced-recovery-after-surgery-eraso-society-recommendations/). Upper-GI cancer resection, respiratory recovery, nutrition and multimodal analgesia.
- **R11.** [BJA Education: Anaesthesia for pancreatic resection surgery, Part 1 (Jarvis, Laing & James, 2025)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11785549/). Pancreatic anatomy, preoperative risks and operation.
- **R12.** [BJA Education: Anaesthesia for pancreatic resection surgery, Part 2 (Jarvis, Laing & James, 2025)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12190887/). Practical intraoperative and perioperative management, complications and recovery.
- **R13.** [ERAS Society: Perioperative care for liver surgery (2022)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9726826/). Low venous-pressure resection phase, haemorrhage, temperature, balanced fluids and recovery; context-specific operative targets.
- **R14.** [BJA Education: Anaesthetic management of abdominal trauma (Edwards et al., 2025)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40083964/). Damage-control resuscitation and surgery, traumatic intra-abdominal bleeding and staged management.
- **R15.** [Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery: Acute mesenteric ischaemia management algorithm (2025)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12363320/). Time-critical diagnosis, arterial versus venous/nonocclusive patterns, CTA and rescue strategy.
- **R16.** [ANZICS: Fourth-edition Statement on Death and Organ Donation (official)](https://www.anzics.org/advocacy/death-organ-donation-dodc/). The Australian/New Zealand legal, ethical and physiological-care standard for deceased-donor retrieval, DBD versus DCD.
- **R17.** [ERAS Society: Bariatric surgery recommendations, 2021 update (published 2022)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8885505/). Respiratory/OSA management, anaesthesia, analgesia, VTE, feeding and micronutrient support.
- **R18.** [2025 European Society for Vascular Surgery mesenteric and renal arteries/veins guideline (PDF)](https://college-vasculaire.com/storage/page_paragraphe/25/page_paragraphe_fichier/68a731c50a3f1354579097d155973e1e.pdf). Current vascular criteria for mesenteric revascularisation and bowel viability assessment; complements the ICU gut-ischaemia chapter.
- **R19.** [ANZCA General Surgical, Urological, Gynaecological and Endoscopic specialised study unit reading guide](https://libguides.anzca.edu.au/anaestrain/ssu/general). Additional ANZCA library resource catalogue; articles are not all interchangeable or fully verified here.
- **R20.** [ERAS Society consensus review: Optimal perioperative care in breast reconstruction (2017)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9074892/). Supports normothermia, balanced goal-directed fluids, appropriate vasopressors, opioid-sparing analgesia and frequent free-flap surveillance.
- **R21.** [ESPEN guideline on clinical nutrition in surgery — update 2025. Applies to early nutrition assessment/feeding in malnourished surgical and major upper-GI populations.](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40957230/).
- **R22.** [Organ Donation New Zealand: current donor documents/forms (reviewed September 2026). Local verification of death documentation, authorisation and procedural checklists.](https://organdonation.govt.nz/docs/documents-and-forms/).
- **R23.** [BJA Education: Anaesthesia for bariatric surgery (Reeve & Kennedy, 2022). Airway, respiratory reserve, OSA/OHS, monitoring and postoperative risk.](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35614907/).
- **R24.** [BJA Education: Ilyas, Jones & Fortey, Management of the patient presenting for emergency laparotomy (2019)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7808094/). Explains emergency laparotomy patient physiology, aspiration, preinduction preparation, risk assessment and the operation sequence; free full text.
- **R25.** [BJA Education: Anaesthesia and sedation for endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (2022)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9482865/). Technique choice, shared/prone airway and conversion/rescue; free full text.
- **R26.** [BJA Education: Patel, Jones & Amoako, Perioperative management for hepatic resection surgery (2022)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9402783/). Segmental anatomy, low-venous-pressure phases, vascular control, future liver remnant, haemostasis and analgesia; free full text.
- **R27.** [BJA Education: Anaesthesia for breast surgery (2018)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7807849/). Breast operative anatomy, reconstruction and regional approaches, including DIEP; free full text.
- **R28.** [BJA Education: Nimalan et al., Anaesthesia for free flap breast reconstruction (2016)](https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaed/mkv036). Microvascular reconstruction and donor/flap perfusion, useful procedural foundation; abstract/landing-page verified, not treated as unrestricted full text.
- **R29.** [BJA Education: Perioperative management of patients with liver disease (2022)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8847800/). Explains decompensated cirrhosis, synthetic function, portal complications and perioperative risk; free full text.
- **R30.** [BJA Education: Acute pain management in patients with severe obesity (2024)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11368600/). Pharmacology, analgesic safety, opioid sensitivity and post-anaesthesia respiratory considerations; free full text.
- **R31.** [ESGE/ESGENA: Sedation for gastrointestinal endoscopy, guideline (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1055/a-2898-6540). Contemporary risk-stratified sedation, monitoring and team/rescue standards; guideline/abstract source verified.
- **R32.** [E-AHPBA–ESSO–Innsbruck consensus recommendations on peri- and postoperative management following liver resection (2025/2026 publication)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12750329/). Up-to-date surveillance/management of bleeding, bile leak, liver failure, antibiotics and thromboprophylaxis; free full text.
- **R33.** [ANZCA 2025.2 and 2026.1 Final Examination Chair reports](https://www.anzca.edu.au/education-and-training/anaesthesia-training-and-pathways/anaesthesia-training-program/anaesthesia-exams). Examiner examples: POEM with oesophageal stasis and failed airway; ERCP with obstructive jaundice and a recent stent; post-Ivor Lewis epidural pain, sepsis, transfer and emergency reoperation. These are examiner outcomes rather than interventional clinical guidelines.

**Additional contemporary sources used for recommendation updates**

- **G1.** [2025 ADS/ANZCA/GESA/NACOS recommendations — GLP-1 and GLP-1/GIP therapies](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12420935)
- **G2.** [Baveno VIII — Advancing consensus in portal hypertension (published 2026)](https://www.journal-of-hepatology.eu/article/S0168-8278%2826%2902778-9/fulltext)
- **G3.** [HeLiX RCT — Tranexamic acid in liver resection (JAMA 2024)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11334013/)
- **G4.** [ASRA Evidence-based guideline (fifth edition, 2025): regional anaesthesia with antithrombotic therapy](https://rapm.bmj.com/content/early/2025/10/16/rapm-2024-105766)
- **G5.** [ERAS Society elective colorectal surgery recommendations (2025)](https://www.surgjournal.com/article/S0039-6060%2825%2900249-1/fulltext)
- **G6.** [ACG guideline on acute pancreatitis (2024)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13221274/)
- **G7.** [Organ Donation New Zealand documents and forms (October 2026 update)](https://organdonation.govt.nz/guidance/documents-and-forms/)
- **G8.** [ANZICS statement on death and organ donation](https://www.anzics.org/advocacy/death-organ-donation-dodc/)
- **G9.** [HALT-IT trial — TXA in gastrointestinal haemorrhage (Lancet 2020)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32563378/)
- **G10.** [ASGE guidance on acute colonic pseudo-obstruction](https://www.asge.org/home/resources/publications/guidelines/american-society-for-gastrointestinal-endoscopy-guideline-on-the-role-of-endoscopy-in-the-management-of-acute-colonic-pseudo-obstruction-and-colonic-volvulus)
- **G11.** [ESGE guideline on peptic ulcer bleeding — 2026 update](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42127996/)
- **G12.** [RELIEF RCT — Restrictive versus liberal fluids in major abdominal surgery, Myles et al. (NEJM 2018)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29742967/)

items.title: What factors increase aspiration risk in a patient with reflux?
items.q: What factors increase aspiration risk in a patient with reflux?
items.a:
- Reduced lower oesophageal sphincter tone and hiatus hernia.
- Obesity, pregnancy, diabetes.
- Opioids and GLP-1 agonists.
- Emergency surgery and bowel obstruction.

items.title: How do you reduce aspiration risk at induction?
items.q: How do you reduce aspiration risk at induction?
items.a: Assess aspiration risk by diagnosis, retained contents, medicines and fasting. Choose awake airway management or a rapid-sequence technique when appropriate, with suction, oxygenation and a rescue plan. Intubation and oxygenation take priority if cricoid pressure interferes.

items.title: How is the severity of liver disease assessed?
items.q: How is the severity of liver disease assessed?
items.a:
- History of complications and treatments.
- Signs of portal hypertension and encephalopathy.
- Bilirubin, albumin, INR, platelets.
- Child–Pugh and MELD scores.

Past exam: 2010.2 Q3

items.title: What are the components of the Child–Pugh score?
items.q: What are the components of the Child–Pugh score?
items.a:
- Bilirubin and albumin.
- INR.
- Ascites.
- Encephalopathy.

Past exam: 2010.2 Q3

items.title: Which extrahepatic complications of cirrhosis matter to the anaesthetist?
items.q: Which extrahepatic complications of cirrhosis matter to the anaesthetist?
items.a:
- Hepatorenal syndrome.
- Hepatopulmonary syndrome and portopulmonary hypertension.
- Cirrhotic cardiomyopathy.
- Coagulopathy and encephalopathy.

Past exam: 2010.2 Q3

items.title: How does liver disease alter drug handling?
items.q: How does liver disease alter drug handling?
items.a:
- Reduced albumin raises free drug.
- Impaired metabolism and larger volume of distribution.
- Avoid morphine and pethidine.
- Use cisatracurium, remifentanil and short-acting agents.

items.title: What is the biochemical result of prolonged gastric vomiting?
items.q: What is the biochemical result of prolonged gastric vomiting?
items.a:
- Hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis.
- Hypokalaemia.
- Volume depletion and hyperaldosteronism.
- Paradoxical aciduria.

items.title: What are the consequences of small bowel obstruction?
items.q: What are the consequences of small bowel obstruction?
items.a:
- Third-space fluid loss and hypovolaemia.
- Electrolyte disturbance.
- Distension impairs ventilation.
- Strangulation causes lactic acidosis and sepsis.

items.title: How do you prepare a patient taking a GLP-1 drug for elective anaesthesia or endoscopy?
items.q: How do you prepare a patient taking a GLP-1 drug for elective anaesthesia or endoscopy?
items.a: Usually continue therapy. Arrange 24 hours of clear fluids and follow ANZCA’s subsequent fasting instructions. If the preparation is inadequate, assess residual gastric content when possible and decide whether to defer or treat as a full stomach.

items.title: How do emergency patients differ from elective patients?
items.q: How do emergency patients differ from elective patients?
items.a:
- Less time to optimise.
- Full stomach and hypovolaemia.
- Higher mortality and sepsis.
- Consent and communication limits.

items.title: What are the perioperative considerations for a patient requiring emergency laparotomy?
items.q: What are the perioperative considerations for a patient requiring emergency laparotomy?
items.a:
## Preop

Resuscitate while planning source control, and assess frailty, aspiration and treatment goals.

## Intraop

Prepare for unstable induction and support oxygenation, perfusion, temperature and analgesia.

## Postop

Handover source control, deterioration triggers and need for critical care.

items.title: What is the differential diagnosis of an acute abdomen?
items.q: What is the differential diagnosis of an acute abdomen?
items.a:

items.title: What anaesthetic problems arise in ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm?

items.a:

items.title: How should a large haematemesis be resuscitated before sedation?
items.q: How should a large haematemesis be resuscitated before sedation?

items.title: What drugs are given in suspected variceal bleeding?

items.title: What is the role of TIPS?

items.title: What are the main hazards of the prone position?
items.q: What are the main hazards of the prone position?

items.title: What are the key steps for turning a patient prone safely?

items.title: Where do you zero the blood pressure transducer in the beach chair position?

items.title: How do you manage hypotension in the beach chair position?

items.title: What patients are poor candidates for prolonged steep head-down surgery?

Check the tube after positioning, limit pressure and tilt as feasible, and maintain ventilation and perfusion.

items.title: How do you prevent airway complications after prolonged head-down surgery?

items.title: What are the cardiovascular effects of pneumoperitoneum?
items.q: What are the cardiovascular effects of pneumoperitoneum?
items.a:
- Raised SVR and MAP.
- Preload falls at IAP above 15 mmHg.
- Cardiac output variable, lower head-up.

items.title: What are the respiratory effects of pneumoperitoneum?
items.q: What are the respiratory effects of pneumoperitoneum?

items.title: How does CO2 absorption affect ventilation?
items.q: How does CO2 absorption affect ventilation?
items.a:
- Absorbed through peritoneum into blood.
- Raises ETCO2 by about 20% in 15 to 30 minutes.

items.title: How does pneumoperitoneum affect renal function?
items.q: How does pneumoperitoneum affect renal function?

items.title: Which immune effects distinguish laparoscopic from open surgery?

items.title: What suggests recurrent bowel ischaemia after vascular intervention?

items.title: How do you manage a seizure associated with rapidly developing postoperative hypotonic hyponatraemia?

items.title: 1. Aspiration risk with obesity and severe reflux
items.q: A patient with obesity, severe symptomatic reflux and a hiatus hernia presents for elective general anaesthesia. Discuss the perioperative considerations for reducing aspiration risk.
items.a:
## Anaesthetic implications

- **Aspiration risk:** the lower oesophageal sphincter is incompetent in severe GORD with a hiatus hernia, and obesity raises intra-abdominal pressure. Regurgitation can occur at induction, during maintenance (particularly with a supraglottic airway or positive pressure) and at emergence. NAP4 found regurgitation at extubation to be a risk in obesity (BJA).
- **Respiratory:** nocturnal aspiration may have caused chronic lung disease, cough or asthma; examine the chest and review spirometry if symptomatic.
- **Airway and OSA:** obesity-related difficulty with mask ventilation and rapid desaturation; screen with STOP-Bang.
- **Drugs:** PPIs, H2 blockers, antacids; smoking, alcohol and caffeine; check for an oesophageal stricture or Barrett's.

## Preop

- Verify the food, fluids and medication history and distinguish standard fasting from delayed emptying or oesophageal retention. Routine liberal clear-fluid pathways are not for all patients with elevated risk. With GLP-1/GIP therapy generally continue it and use a 24-hour clear-fluid diet followed by the ANZCA fasting instructions. If the pathway has not been completed, assess gastric content where appropriate, defer elective care if needed or manage as a full stomach.
- Premedication: a non-particulate antacid (sodium citrate) and an H2 blocker or PPI on the morning of surgery; metoclopramide where gastric emptying is slow.
- Gastric ultrasound by a trained clinician may identify solids or increased gastric volume. A reassuring gastric image does not exclude a retained oesophageal bolus or remove other sources of aspiration risk.

## Intraop

- Ramped position and preoxygenation to an end-tidal oxygen of 90% (BJA).
- If the stomach is considered full: **rapid sequence induction** with a pre-induction vasopressor plan, rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg or suxamethonium, and a cuffed tracheal tube, with suction ready; apply cricoid pressure only if it does not impair the view. Avoid a supraglottic airway for a high-risk patient.
- Maintain the tube cuff pressure and use PEEP.

## Postop

Extubate awake, upright and with the stomach suctioned, and keep the patient on a head-up tilt in recovery.

## If aspiration occurs

Suction, prioritise oxygenation and airway protection, and use supportive ventilation. Consider selective bronchoscopy for obstructing particulate material. Evaluate bacterial infection and other indications before prescribing antibiotics.

Confirm the recovery position and monitoring before transfer of care.

**Sources:** [ANZCA GLP-1 and GLP-1/GIP recommendations](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/standards-of-practice/clinical-practice-recommendations-regarding-patients-taking-glp-1) · [ANZCA 2027 Blue Book preview on severe aspiration](https://airr.anzca.edu.au/anzcacrisjspui/handle/11055/1402) · [ANZCA professional documents including PG09, PG07 and PG56](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/standards-of-practice/professional-documents)

## Self-marking checklist

- Why GORD and obesity raise aspiration risk, including at emergence
- Respiratory and OSA assessment
- Fasting plan and Sip Til Send principle
- GLP-1 agonist guidance (ask, do not routinely cease, 24 hour fluids)
- Antacid, H2 blocker or PPI premedication
- Gastric ultrasound grades and interpretation
- Ramped position, preoxygenation and rapid sequence induction
- Extubation awake and upright; management if aspiration occurs

items.title: 2. Child–Pugh B cirrhosis with ascites for hernia repair
items.q: A patient with Child–Pugh B cirrhosis and ascites is being considered for elective inguinal hernia repair. Discuss the perioperative implications and management.
items.a:
## Implications of Child-Pugh B cirrhosis with ascites

Estimate risk using severity, prior decompensation and the proposed operation. Child–Pugh and MELD aid staging. Add a surgery-specific estimate such as VOCAL-Penn when applicable. Discuss ascites control, frailty, elective timing and alternatives with hepatology and surgery. A single score does not define operability.

**Systems**
- **Circulation:** hyperdynamic with low SVR; alcoholic cardiomyopathy; vasopressors may be needed.
- **Lungs:** ascites reduces functional residual capacity and may change aspiration risk. Investigate suspected hepatopulmonary syndrome or portopulmonary hypertension selectively. Echocardiography is a screening test for pulmonary hypertension.
- **Kidneys:** hepatorenal syndrome risk; avoid hypovolaemia, NSAIDs and nephrotoxins.
- **Coagulation:** platelets low from hypersplenism and reduced synthetic function, but the INR does not predict bleeding; do not give plasma for the INR alone; use viscoelastic testing.
- **Brain:** encephalopathy, sedatives worsen it.
- **Ascites and electrolytes:** hyponatraemia, hypokalaemia; tense ascites may need paracentesis.
- **Varices:** check whether banding has been done; avoid raising portal pressure.

## Preop

grade the disease (Child-Pugh, MELD), review the albumin, bilirubin, platelets, renal function, and sodium, with an echocardiogram. Continue beta blocker and diuretics carefully, treat infection and give vitamin K if prolonged.

## Intraop

- **Neuraxial block** is not recommended unless coagulation is corrected (Blue Book 2017). Spinal anaesthesia for a hernia is often considered but risks haematoma and hypotension.
- Consider local or regional approaches, where appropriate, or general anaesthesia with a cuffed airway when aspiration risk warrants it. Titrate drugs to haemodynamics and organ function.
- **Drugs:** avoid pethidine; fentanyl and remifentanil are largely unaffected; use cisatracurium or atracurium; paracetamol 2 to 3 g a day for long-term use.
- **Analgesia:** a local anaesthetic wound infiltration or an ilioinguinal or TAP block, with maximum doses reduced (peak plasma level about 30 minutes, up to 90 minutes, Blue Book 2017 abdominal wall blocks).
- **Haemodynamics:** MAP at baseline; avoid hypotension and hypovolaemia; give balanced crystalloid and albumin if large-volume paracentesis is done.
- **Thromboprophylaxis** should not be omitted.

## Postop

HDU, watch for encephalopathy, renal impairment, wound leak of ascites, and infection.

Before operating, optimise ascites, nutrition and reversible kidney or electrolyte problems. Suspected spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, AKI or active encephalopathy warrants review and usually deferral of a nonurgent operation. Discuss whether ongoing ascites changes recurrence and wound risks.

**Sources:** [EASL extrahepatic abdominal surgery in cirrhosis guideline 2025](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0168827825002351) · [BJA Education perioperative management of liver disease](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35211328/) · [Baveno VIII portal hypertension consensus](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42624290/)

## Self-marking checklist

- Quotes mortality by Child-Pugh class and MELD threshold
- Indication and optimisation for elective surgery
- Hyperdynamic circulation, hepatopulmonary and portopulmonary syndromes
- Hepatorenal risk and renal protection
- Coagulation: platelets, INR does not predict bleeding
- Neuraxial block caveat and general anaesthesia with rapid sequence induction if ascites is tense
- Drug choices and paracetamol limits
- Local anaesthetic dosing, HDU and encephalopathy monitoring

items.title: 3. Consequences of prolonged vomiting and obstruction
items.q: Outline the metabolic and physiological consequences of prolonged vomiting and bowel obstruction, and how they affect your preoperative management.
items.a:
## Consequences

**Prolonged vomiting (high obstruction or gastric outlet obstruction)**
- Loss of gastric hydrochloric acid causes a **hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis** (alkalaemia, BJA). Volume depletion activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, which conserves sodium and bicarbonate and wastes potassium and hydrogen ions in the urine ("paradoxical aciduria"). Hyponatraemia, hypomagnesaemia and ionised hypocalcaemia can follow.

**Bowel obstruction (distal)**
- Fluid sequestration in the bowel lumen and wall (third space) causes **hypovolaemia**, prerenal acute kidney injury and haemoconcentration; loss of bicarbonate-rich secretions and later ischaemia or sepsis cause **metabolic acidosis and raised lactate**, which warns of strangulation.
- Raised intra-abdominal pressure impairs ventilation and venous return, and bacterial translocation causes sepsis.

**Mixed picture:** acid-base status depends on the level and duration; the gas, anion gap and lactate guide the analysis.

**Airway:** vomiting and distension produce a **full stomach** and a high aspiration risk, whatever the fasting time (BJA).

## Effect on preoperative management

- **1.** **Assess volume and perfusion:** heart rate, blood pressure, capillary refill, urine output, lactate, urea and creatinine; recognise that a normal blood pressure may hide significant depletion.
- **2.** **Resuscitate before induction as time allows:** balanced crystalloid (the Blue Book on emergency laparotomy supports it) because saline worsens hyperchloraemia; give potassium cautiously, with monitoring, and correct magnesium and calcium. Use an arterial line.
- **3.** **Check investigations:** electrolytes, bicarbonate, glucose, full blood count, group and screen, and coagulation; ECG for the effects of hypokalaemia.
- **4.** **Decompress the stomach** with a nasogastric tube and aspirate before induction.
- **5.** **Plan the induction:** rapid sequence induction with a reduced dose and a vasopressor ready, because induction on a depleted patient causes hypotension; avoid suxamethonium if potassium is high.
- **6.** **Timing:** if there are signs of strangulation, perforation or sepsis, do not delay surgery for correction; resuscitate in parallel.
- **7.** **Postoperative:** HDU, continued fluid and electrolyte management, and monitoring for refeeding problems if the fasting was prolonged.

The pattern depends on the site and duration. Ongoing gastric hydrogen and chloride losses cause chloride-depletion alkalosis with potassium depletion. Advanced obstruction or ischaemia can add lactic acidosis, so a near-normal pH can conceal a mixed disorder. Assess serial gas and electrolytes, urine losses and perfusion. Treat chloride-responsive alkalosis with fluid and chloride replacement as indicated, and reassess before induction rather than normalising all results while a time-critical abdomen deteriorates.

**Sources:** [BJA Education pancreatic resection Part 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12190887/) · [ANZCA 2025 Blue Book emergency laparotomy chapter](https://anzca.intersearch.com.au/anzcacrisjspui/handle/11055/1386)

## Self-marking checklist

- Gastric loss produces hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria
- Distal obstruction causes hypovolaemia, acidosis and lactate rise
- Raised intra-abdominal pressure and sepsis
- Full stomach regardless of fasting
- Volume assessment and resuscitation with balanced crystalloid
- Potassium, magnesium and calcium correction
- Nasogastric decompression and rapid sequence induction with reduced doses
- Timing versus delay and postoperative monitoring

items.title: 4. Emergency laparotomy for small bowel obstruction
items.q: A 72-year-old man with three days of vomiting and distension needs emergency laparotomy for suspected bowel obstruction. Discuss the perioperative considerations.
items.a:
## Preop

A 72-year-old with 3 days of vomiting and distension has dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, possible ischaemia or perforation and a full stomach.
- **Risk:** 30-day mortality after emergency laparotomy is 5 to 20% (ANZELA 5.2%), median age 66. A documented preoperative risk assessment is associated with lower mortality (9.5% without versus 5.2% with, Perth audit). Use a score such as NELA (13 variables, AUROC 0.861) or P-POSSUM, and record the risk.
- Arrange source control as soon as feasible when shock, perforation or threatened bowel is present. Use appropriate antibiotics for suspected sepsis and review imaging with senior surgery. An unstable patient needing immediate surgery should not wait for nonessential tests.
- **Frailty and goals of care:** assess frailty, discuss the likely outcomes, and consider a "No-Lap" or limited treatment decision. Control glucose (8 to 10) and avoid sedatives.
- **Team:** consultant anaesthetist and surgeon involved; book a direct ICU bed if the risk is 10% or more (ANZELA) or 5% or more (NELA).

**Resuscitation and induction**

- Large-bore access and an **arterial line before induction**; correct hypovolaemia and potassium; start noradrenaline early for septic patients.
- **Full stomach:** an NG tube to decompress, then rapid sequence induction with suxamethonium or rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg, preoxygenation and a reduced-dose induction agent with a pre-induction fluid bolus and vasopressor ready.

## Intraop

- **Ventilation:** lung-protective; high airway pressures with hypoxia suggest abdominal compartment syndrome.
- Use balanced crystalloid, titrated vasopressors and blood products as indicated. Individualise perfusion goals. If bleeding is substantial, identify the source and use the local major haemorrhage pathway.
- **Analgesia:** opioids first line with TAP or rectus blocks; epidural may be contraindicated in sepsis; avoid NSAIDs in older patients.
- **Other:** warming, glucose, neuromuscular monitoring and a plan for the abdomen to be left open.

## Postop

Extubate awake if ventilation and haemodynamics permit. Plan ICU if support is needed. Follow shock, fluid losses, AKI, electrolytes, stoma function and surgical source control. Provide an early recovery, nutrition and delirium prevention plan as physiology allows.

Correct important potassium, chloride and volume deficits in parallel with preparation. A functioning nasogastric tube can reduce distension without excluding gastric retention. Reassess obstruction severity and aspiration risk immediately before induction.

**Sources:** [ANZCA 2025 Blue Book emergency laparotomy chapter](https://anzca.intersearch.com.au/anzcacrisjspui/handle/11055/1386) · [ERAS Society emergency laparotomy Part 2](https://www.erassociety.org/guideline/consensus-guidelines-for-perioperative-care-for-emergency-laparotomy-enhanced-recovery-after-surgery-eras-society-recommendations-part-2-emergency-laparotomy-intra-and-postoperative/)

## Self-marking checklist

- Preoperative risk assessment with a score and quoted mortality
- Source control timing for septic shock and for sepsis without shock
- Frailty, goals of care and ICU planning thresholds
- Arterial line and noradrenaline before induction
- Full stomach: NG decompression and rapid sequence induction details
- Lung-protective ventilation and abdominal compartment syndrome
- Fluids, MAP, haemoglobin and tranexamic acid targets
- Analgesia options with sepsis caveats, extubation and postoperative care

items.title: 5. Differential diagnosis of the acute abdomen
items.q: Outline the differential diagnosis of the acute abdomen and explain how it changes the perioperative considerations.
items.a:
## Differential diagnosis by category

- **Perforation or obstruction:** perforated peptic ulcer, diverticulitis, appendicitis, bowel obstruction (adhesions, hernia, volvulus, malignancy), and anastomotic leak.
- **Ischaemia and vascular:** mesenteric ischaemia, ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm, aortic dissection, and ischaemic colitis.
- **Haemorrhagic:** ruptured aneurysm, ectopic pregnancy, splenic or hepatic injury, and haemorrhagic pancreatitis.
- **Inflammatory and biliary:** cholecystitis, cholangitis, pancreatitis, and inflammatory bowel disease.
- **Gynaecological and urological:** ectopic pregnancy, torsion, renal colic, and pelvic inflammatory disease.
- **Medical mimics:** myocardial infarction, diabetic ketoacidosis, pneumonia, and porphyria.

## Preop

**Urgency and timing:** The Blue Book gives source control within 3 hours for septic shock and within 6 hours for sepsis without shock, and imaging should not delay surgery. A ruptured aneurysm, ischaemic bowel and haemorrhage need immediate surgery; obstruction can allow some resuscitation.

**Resuscitation and monitoring:** large-bore access and arterial line before induction, balanced crystalloids, blood for haemorrhage, noradrenaline in sepsis.

**Airway:** a full stomach in obstruction, ileus and peritonitis, so decompress and perform a rapid sequence induction. Gastric outlet obstruction is treated as a full stomach regardless of fasting (BJA).

**Physiology by cause**
- Sepsis: vasodilatation and fluid shifts; noradrenaline early; antibiotics; neuraxial block may be contraindicated.
- Haemorrhage (aneurysm, ectopic): permissive hypotension until control, a massive transfusion protocol and cell salvage; avoid dilutional coagulopathy.
- Ischaemia: lactic acidosis, reperfusion injury and the risk of a second look.
- Obstruction: dehydration, electrolyte disturbance and aspiration.
- Pancreatitis, cholangitis: organ failure, sepsis, jaundice effects (BJA).
- Pregnancy or gynaecological: confirm pregnancy status.

**Risk and goals:** use NELA or P-POSSUM and document, assess frailty, and agree goals of care and the ICU plan before induction (Blue Book).

**Technique:** consultant presence, lung-protective ventilation, multimodal analgesia (opioids first, TAP or rectus blocks, avoid NSAIDs in the elderly), temperature management and glucose control.

## Intraop

Match induction, ventilation, perfusion support and monitoring to the diagnosis. Prepare blood for haemorrhage and request antibiotics and source control for perforation or sepsis. If gut ischaemia is suspected, coordinate possible revascularisation and bowel assessment, anticipating reperfusion-related acidaemia, hyperkalaemia and instability. Reassess the need for damage-control surgery when physiology deteriorates.

## Postop

HDU or ICU for risk of 10% or more (ANZELA), early review by the surgeon, geriatric input, and early feeding where possible.

**Sources:** [ANZCA 2025 Blue Book emergency laparotomy chapter](https://anzca.intersearch.com.au/anzcacrisjspui/handle/11055/1386) · [ERAS Society emergency laparotomy Part 2](https://www.erassociety.org/guideline/consensus-guidelines-for-perioperative-care-for-emergency-laparotomy-enhanced-recovery-after-surgery-eras-society-recommendations-part-2-emergency-laparotomy-intra-and-postoperative/)

## Self-marking checklist

- Differential by category: perforation or obstruction, ischaemia, haemorrhage, inflammatory, gynaecological, mimics
- Urgency and source control timing
- Resuscitation, monitoring and full stomach
- Cause-specific physiology (sepsis, haemorrhage, ischaemia, obstruction)
- Risk scoring, frailty and goals of care
- Analgesia and technique choices
- Postoperative destination and review
- Medical mimics and pregnancy status

items.title: 6. Haematemesis: resuscitation and endoscopy
items.q: A 58-year-old man presents with haematemesis and haemodynamic instability. Outline resuscitation and perioperative considerations for urgent therapeutic endoscopy.
items.a:
## Preop

- **Airway and access:** two large-bore cannulae and an arterial line if shocked; send group and crossmatch, full blood count, coagulation, fibrinogen, urea and creatinine, glucose, lactate and calcium, and use viscoelastic testing.
- In active shock transfuse for physiology and ongoing losses with the major haemorrhage protocol when indicated. Once stabilised, use a restrictive approach with individualisation for ischaemia and comorbidity. Avoid plasma to normalise INR alone in cirrhosis, and guide products by clinical bleeding and tests.
- **Fluids:** balanced crystalloid and blood early, with noradrenaline if needed. In a patient with varices, over-resuscitation raises portal pressure and rebleeding.

## Find the cause

Variceal bleeding is likely with cirrhosis or alcohol use; otherwise peptic ulcer, Mallory-Weiss tear or erosive disease. Risk stratify (Glasgow-Blatchford, from memory).
- **Variceal:** start early vasoactive therapy and antibiotic prophylaxis, and consider erythromycin if appropriate. Band oesophageal varices and tailor gastric variceal intervention by subtype. Arrange early TIPS assessment for eligible high-risk patients. If bleeding remains uncontrolled use specialist-led bridge therapy with a secured airway.
- **Non-variceal:** IV PPI, endoscopic therapy (adrenaline injection, clips, thermal), and repeat endoscopy or radiological embolisation for rebleeding. Tranexamic acid is not routinely helpful (HALT-IT, from memory).

## Intraop

- **Airway decision:** the Blue Book bases sedation versus general anaesthesia on aspiration risk, airway protection and respiratory reserve. Active haematemesis, encephalopathy or shock favours **general anaesthesia with rapid sequence induction after resuscitation**, with head-up positioning, large-bore suction and a reduced-dose induction agent with a vasopressor ready (ketamine or etomidate, rocuronium or suxamethonium).
- **Liver and alcohol:** reduced drug doses, avoid pethidine, check for ascites, encephalopathy and renal impairment, and treat withdrawal with thiamine and benzodiazepines (BJA, Blue Book).
- **Timing:** endoscopy within 12 hours for variceal bleeding once resuscitated; earlier if unstable (Blue Book).

## Postop

Use ICU when shock, ongoing ventilation or organ dysfunction warrants it. Continue indicated vasoactive and antibiotic treatment with reassessment. Document the haemostatic result and contingency for rebleeding. For high-risk ulcer bleeding arrange PPI and a repeat endoscopy or embolisation plan as appropriate.

The initial haemoglobin can remain normal during severe acute loss. Follow the clinical response and trends and distinguish shock resuscitation from the later maintenance transfusion strategy.

**Sources:** [Baveno VIII portal hypertension consensus](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42624290/) · [ESGE peptic ulcer bleeding guideline 2026](https://doi.org/10.1055/a-2863-8314) · [HALT-IT trial](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(20)30848-5)

## Self-marking checklist

- Large-bore access, arterial line, bloods and viscoelastic testing
- Restrictive transfusion at about 70 g/L and targets for MAP, temperature and calcium
- No routine plasma or platelets; use fibrinogen or prothrombin complex concentrate
- Uses an early vasoactive and antibiotic bundle and source-specific endoscopic therapy
- Balloon tamponade needs intubation; TIPS rescue
- Non-variceal management and risk scoring
- Sedation versus general anaesthesia decision with rapid sequence induction
- Liver and alcohol considerations and post-endoscopy care

items.title: 7. Perioperative hypothermia: causes and consequences
items.q: Discuss the causes and consequences of perioperative hypothermia in a patient undergoing a prolonged open laparotomy, and the measures you would take to prevent it.
items.a:
## Causes in a prolonged laparotomy

Hypothermia is a core temperature below 36 degrees and is almost universal in major abdominal surgery without active warming:
- **Redistribution** after induction: vasodilatation moves heat from the core to the periphery (a fall of about 1 degree in the first hour).
- **Heat loss** from the exposed viscera (evaporation, radiation, convection) in a cold theatre, and from cold skin preparation.
- **Cold IV fluids, blood and irrigation fluid**, and dry unwarmed ventilation gases.
- **Impaired thermoregulation** from anaesthesia, neuraxial block and muscle relaxants, and low heat production.
- **Patient factors:** age, low weight, sepsis or shock, hypothyroidism.

## Consequences

- **Coagulopathy:** platelet dysfunction and reduced clotting factor enzymes, increasing blood loss and transfusion. The Blue Books use a temperature above 35 degrees as a resuscitation target in bleeding (2023 portal hypertension).
- **Cardiovascular:** arrhythmia, increased afterload, myocardial ischaemia, and shivering that raises oxygen use by up to 400%.
- **Infection and healing:** vasoconstriction lowers wound oxygen tension, increasing surgical site infection.
- **Drugs:** slower metabolism of muscle relaxants and anaesthetic drugs, with delayed emergence.
- **Metabolic:** acidosis, hyperglycaemia, shift of the oxygen curve to the left and impaired renal function.
- **Other:** delayed recovery, increased ICU stay, and patient discomfort.

## Prevention

- **Monitor core temperature** (oesophageal, nasopharyngeal or bladder) throughout; skin temperature is unreliable. ERAS requires maintenance of normothermia (BJA).
- **Prewarm** for 15 to 30 minutes (forced air) where practical, and keep the theatre warm during preparation and drape-up.
- **Intraoperative:** forced-air warming over exposed areas, a warming mattress, warmed IV fluids and blood through a fluid warmer, warmed irrigation fluid, humidified and heated breathing circuit, limit exposure, and consider a low fresh gas flow.
- **Recovery:** continue warming, treat shivering with pethidine or clonidine, and recheck the temperature before discharge from recovery.
- **Rewarming:** active rewarming of a hypothermic patient is more effective than passive, and avoid rapid peripheral vasodilatation that causes afterdrop.

Check a reliable core measurement site and track trends across transfers. Use active surface warming, warmed IV fluids and blood as indicated, conserve exposed surface and avoid unnecessary delays. In recovery continue warming until clinically appropriate. If hypothermia persists despite equipment and treatment, assess other causes such as ongoing bleeding, hypoperfusion or severe infection.

**Sources:** [ERAS Society emergency laparotomy Part 2](https://www.erassociety.org/guideline/consensus-guidelines-for-perioperative-care-for-emergency-laparotomy-enhanced-recovery-after-surgery-eras-society-recommendations-part-2-emergency-laparotomy-intra-and-postoperative/) · [ERAS Society recommendations for liver surgery](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00268-022-06732-5)

## Self-marking checklist

- Redistribution, exposure, cold fluids and anaesthetic effects as causes
- Coagulopathy and bleeding consequences with temperature target
- Cardiovascular consequences and shivering
- Wound infection and delayed drug metabolism
- Core temperature monitoring
- Prewarming and forced-air warming
- Warmed fluids, humidified gas and theatre temperature
- Recovery warming and active rewarming

items.title: 8. Metabolic acidosis during a prolonged laparotomy
items.q: During a prolonged laparotomy for a bowel resection you note a metabolic acidosis (pH 7.22, bicarbonate 14 mmol/L, base excess −12). Discuss the differential diagnosis and your management.
items.a:
## Interpretation

pH 7.22, bicarbonate 14 and base excess −12 is a **metabolic acidosis**. Check the PaCO2 and calculate the expected compensation (Winter's formula: 1.5 × 14 + 8 = 29 mmHg, ±2). If the measured PaCO2 is higher, there is a concurrent respiratory acidosis (for example hypoventilation under anaesthesia); if lower, a respiratory alkalosis. Then calculate the **anion gap** (sodium − chloride − bicarbonate; correct for albumin) and the delta ratio.

## Differential diagnosis in a laparotomy for bowel resection

**High anion gap**
- **Lactic acidosis** from hypoperfusion or sepsis, bowel ischaemia or necrosis, hypovolaemia, vasopressors, mesenteric clamping, hepatic dysfunction, and metformin.
- **Ketoacidosis:** diabetic, starvation or alcoholic; **euglycaemic ketoacidosis** with an SGLT2 inhibitor, particularly after fasting (Blue Book 2019).
- **Renal failure**, toxins (methanol, ethylene glycol, salicylate) and rhabdomyolysis.

**Normal anion gap**
