- **Hyperchloraemic acidosis** from large volumes of 0.9% saline, which is why the Blue Book on emergency laparotomy recommends balanced crystalloids.
- **Bicarbonate loss:** diarrhoea, ileostomy or small bowel fistula, pancreatic fluid loss, and renal tubular acidosis.

**Mixed:** often multiple causes, for example a lactic acidosis plus a saline-induced acidosis.

## Management

- **1.** **Assess the patient:** haemodynamics, perfusion, temperature and blood loss. Confirm the gas with a repeat sample and measure lactate, ketones, glucose, electrolytes, creatinine and chloride.
- **2.** **Treat the cause:** restore perfusion with fluids (balanced crystalloid), blood if bleeding, vasopressors, inotropes; ask the surgeon to look for ischaemic bowel, perforation and an undrained abscess; obtain **source control** and give antibiotics (Blue Book: within 3 hours in septic shock).
- **3.** **Ketoacidosis:** an insulin infusion with glucose, potassium replacement and fluids.
- **4.** **Ventilation:** keep the compensatory minute volume rather than lowering it; the patient cannot compensate while paralysed, so increase the minute ventilation to match.
- **5.** **Bicarbonate:** consider only for severe acidosis (pH below about 7.1 to 7.2) with haemodynamic effects or severe hyperkalaemia, because it generates CO2 and does not treat the cause.
- **6.** **Electrolytes:** replace potassium, magnesium and ionised calcium.
- **7.** **Renal replacement** if the acidosis is refractory, with kidney injury or fluid overload.
- **8.** **Postoperative:** ICU, serial gases and lactate.

Compare measured PaCO₂ to expected respiratory compensation and use lactate, chloride, ketones, renal function and operative findings to identify mixed causes. Severe acidosis should trigger review of source control and immediate perfusion, including haemorrhage or ischaemic bowel.

**Sources:** [ANZCA 2025 Blue Book emergency laparotomy chapter](https://anzca.intersearch.com.au/anzcacrisjspui/handle/11055/1386) · [ERAS Society emergency laparotomy Part 2](https://www.erassociety.org/guideline/consensus-guidelines-for-perioperative-care-for-emergency-laparotomy-enhanced-recovery-after-surgery-eras-society-recommendations-part-2-emergency-laparotomy-intra-and-postoperative/)

## Self-marking checklist

- Identifies metabolic acidosis and checks compensation with Winter formula
- Anion gap and delta ratio
- High-gap causes: lactate, ketones including SGLT2 euglycaemic ketoacidosis, renal, toxins
- Normal-gap causes: saline, bicarbonate loss
- Treat the cause: perfusion, source control, antibiotics
- Insulin and electrolyte management for ketoacidosis
- Match minute ventilation to compensation
- Judicious bicarbonate use and renal replacement

items.title: 9. Aspiration at induction for emergency bowel surgery
items.q: During induction for emergency bowel surgery, the patient aspirates food particles and develops severe hypoxaemia. Outline your immediate management and explain when bronchoscopy may help.
items.a:
## Immediate airway and oxygenation

Call for help, ask surgery to pause and give high-concentration oxygen. Suction visible material from the mouth and pharynx promptly. If safe, position to reduce further contamination without delaying oxygenation or tracheal intubation. Establish a cuffed tracheal tube and confirm capnography. Suction through the tube as indicated. Ensure tube and circuit patency, and assess for endobronchial intubation, major bronchospasm, pneumothorax and obstruction by particulate material. Where positive-pressure ventilation is necessary to maintain oxygenation, give it. A severely hypoxaemic patient cannot wait for an ideal sequence. Treat haemodynamic compromise alongside respiratory support.

## Decide whether to use bronchoscopy

Large particles can obstruct a bronchus or prevent ventilation despite routine suction. Persistent hypoxaemia, unexplained high airway pressures, asymmetric breath sounds or lobar collapse after witnessed particulate aspiration support urgent specialist discussion. Flexible bronchoscopy can locate material and guide suction or extraction. Large proximal obstruction may require a different bronchoscopic approach and specialist resources. The 2027 ANZCA Blue Book preview describes bronchoalveolar toileting for selected severe aspiration. This is technique-focused material, with limited comparative outcomes evidence. Routine lavage after a small liquid aspiration is not established and can worsen hypoxaemia or redistribute material. Discuss the likely benefit, expertise, oxygenation and ability to ventilate during the procedure. Stabilise the patient and avoid delays in airway control or urgent surgery.

## Ongoing care

Use lung-protective ventilation and appropriate PEEP if lung injury develops. Obtain blood gas and chest imaging as indicated, recognising that early imaging can be unremarkable. Treat bronchospasm and reassess perfusion. The immediate inflammatory syndrome can be chemical pneumonitis. Antibiotics are not routine solely for uncomplicated chemical aspiration, but assess aspiration content, concurrent abdominal sepsis and evidence of bacterial infection. Steroids are not routine. Discuss whether to continue surgery based on source-control urgency and physiological stability. Consider postoperative ICU and ventilatory support, clinical trajectory and evolving infection or ARDS. Document the event, arrange open disclosure and hand over aspirate type, ventilation, bronchoscopy findings and planned escalation. Review whether obstruction, fasting limitations or the airway plan contributed.

Revisit aspiration precautions, document the airway plan and check residual respiratory support if the patient returns to theatre during the same admission.

**Sources:** [ANZCA 2027 Blue Book preview on severe aspiration](https://airr.anzca.edu.au/anzcacrisjspui/handle/11055/1402) · [ERAS Society emergency laparotomy Part 2](https://www.erassociety.org/guideline/consensus-guidelines-for-perioperative-care-for-emergency-laparotomy-enhanced-recovery-after-surgery-eras-society-recommendations-part-2-emergency-laparotomy-intra-and-postoperative/)

## Self-marking checklist

- Prioritises suction, oxygenation and a cuffed airway
- Recognises obstruction, bronchospasm and alternative causes
- Identifies selective bronchoscopy for particulate obstruction
- Avoids routine lavage or delays to rescue
- Distinguishes chemical injury and infection
- Plans ICU, surgery decision and disclosure

items.title: 10. Cholangitis with sepsis needing urgent decompression
items.q: An 80-year-old woman with sepsis from acute cholangitis requires urgent biliary decompression. Discuss the perioperative considerations.
items.a:
## Preop

An 80-year-old with sepsis from acute cholangitis has obstruction of the bile duct with infection and bacteraemia, and a high risk of death. Grade severity (Tokyo guidelines: grade III has organ dysfunction, from memory) and recognise that **urgent decompression is the definitive treatment**.

**Effects to anticipate (BJA jaundice list):** haemodynamic instability, acute kidney injury, myocardial depression, coagulopathy, immunosuppression and poor healing. Add frailty, cognitive impairment, polypharmacy, dehydration, and possible delirium.

**Resuscitation and preparation**

- **Sepsis bundle:** blood cultures then broad-spectrum antibiotics immediately, balanced crystalloid, early noradrenaline for septic shock (Blue Book), lactate, and an arterial line.
- Arrange urgent biliary drainage alongside resuscitation. In shock coordinate endoscopy, interventional radiology and ICU promptly. Obtain additional imaging only when it will guide management without delaying necessary drainage.
- **Coagulopathy:** IV vitamin K; avoid plasma for the INR alone (Blue Book 2017), and use viscoelastic testing if bleeding.
- **Renal:** avoid nephrotoxins and hypotension; monitor urine output.
- **Frailty and goals of care:** assess baseline function, discuss treatment limits and plan ICU or HDU based on shock, respiratory reserve and anticipated organ support.

## Intraop

- **Options:** endoscopic drainage is usually preferred. If ERCP is unavailable, impossible or unsuccessful, discuss alternative image-guided drainage. In severe instability use the least burdensome effective initial decompression, with definitive treatment later where indicated.
- **Anaesthetic choice:** a septic, elderly patient in a semi-prone position with a shared airway is best managed with **general anaesthesia and a cuffed tube**, rapid sequence induction if vomiting or ileus, reduced doses with vasopressor support, and an arterial line. A light sedation is an option only for a stable patient.
- **Drugs:** reduced doses; avoid pethidine, limit paracetamol, and use fentanyl or remifentanil and cisatracurium or atracurium (Blue Book 2017).
- **Ventilation and temperature:** lung-protective ventilation, warming and glucose control.

## Postop

Return to ICU or HDU for vasopressor weaning and organ support. Continue antibiotics based on cultures, watch for a post-ERCP complication (pancreatitis, perforation, bleeding), manage delirium (avoid benzodiazepines, treat pain, orient), and prepare for definitive cholecystectomy if appropriate.

When sedation is considered, evaluate ability to cooperate, work of breathing, duration, airway contamination and ability to rescue in the planned position. Confirm equipment, trained support, transfer route and resuscitation access before induction.

**Sources:** [BJA Education anaesthesia and sedation for ERCP](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9482865/) · [BJA consensus for ERCP](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bja.2023.03.012)

## Self-marking checklist

- Recognise cholangitis severity and that urgent decompression is definitive
- Effects of jaundice and age to anticipate
- Sepsis bundle with antibiotics, fluids and early noradrenaline
- Source control timing (3 hours and 6 hours)
- Coagulopathy management without plasma for INR alone
- Frailty and goals of care with ICU planning
- Anaesthetic choice with airway and drug adjustments
- Postoperative organ support and delirium prevention

items.title: 11. Oesophageal perforation after forceful vomiting
items.q: A 60-year-old man presents with severe chest pain and subcutaneous emphysema after forceful vomiting. Outline the diagnosis and management of oesophageal perforation.
items.a:
## Diagnosis

This is **Boerhaave's syndrome** (spontaneous rupture of the distal oesophagus after forceful vomiting): the history, severe chest or upper abdominal pain, and subcutaneous emphysema. Mackler's triad is vomiting, chest pain and subcutaneous emphysema. Other features are fever, dyspnoea, tachycardia, shock and a pleural effusion (left more often). Other causes: iatrogenic (endoscopy, dilatation, tube placement, bougie), foreign body, trauma, and malignancy.

**Differential:** myocardial infarction, aortic dissection, pulmonary embolism, perforated peptic ulcer and pneumothorax.

**Investigations:** chest radiograph (pneumomediastinum, pleural effusion, hydropneumothorax), and **CT chest and abdomen with oral water-soluble contrast**, which is the investigation of choice and shows the leak and collections. A contrast swallow or endoscopy can add information. Bloods: white cells, CRP, lactate, gas, creatinine and an ECG with troponin to exclude infarction.

## Management

Mortality rises with time to treatment (higher if more than 24 hours).

- **1.** **Resuscitate and treat sepsis:** nil by mouth, access, balanced crystalloid and prompt antibiotics covering appropriate Gram-positive, Gram-negative and anaerobic organisms. Antifungal treatment is selective and guided by risk and microbiology. Start a vasopressor if indicated and arrange urgent source control.
- **2.** **Pleural drainage** of effusion or pneumothorax.
- **3.** **Definitive treatment (surgical decision):**
   - Early (under 24 hours): primary repair with buttressing and wide drainage, or drainage with an oesophageal stent.
   - Late or unfit: drainage with a covered self-expanding stent, endoscopic clips or vacuum therapy; oesophagectomy or exclusion for extensive damage.
- **4.** **Nutrition:** a feeding jejunostomy or parenteral support.

## Anaesthetic considerations

- **Airway:** a full stomach with mediastinal contamination; rapid sequence induction with a pre-induction vasopressor plan.
- **Ventilation:** positive pressure can enlarge a pneumothorax or pneumomediastinum, so have a chest drain ready; for repair via a thoracotomy use a double-lumen tube and one-lung ventilation, protecting the repair.
- **Tubes:** do not pass a nasogastric tube blind (the bariatric article warns of perforation with blind passage of large tubes).
- **Monitoring:** arterial line, central line, urine output.
- **Postoperative:** ICU with sepsis care, a protective analgesia plan, and a contrast study before oral intake.

Involve upper-GI surgery promptly. Stable, contained cases may be considered for selected nonoperative or endoscopic treatment with specialist surveillance. An unstable patient, free leak or major contamination usually requires urgent operative or interventional source control. Reassess nutrition and drainage with ICU and the treating team.

**Sources:** [WSES oesophageal emergencies guideline](https://doi.org/10.1186/s13017-019-0245-2)

## Self-marking checklist

- Recognise Boerhaave syndrome and its causes
- Clinical features and Mackler triad
- Differential diagnosis including cardiac, aortic and pulmonary causes
- CT with oral water-soluble contrast and supporting investigations
- Resuscitation and sepsis care including antifungal and source control timing
- Surgical options by timing: repair, drainage, stent
- Anaesthetic airway and one-lung ventilation considerations
- Avoid blind nasogastric tubes; ICU care

items.title: 12. Sleep apnoea and heart disease for gastroscopy and colonoscopy
items.q: A 75-year-old with obstructive sleep apnoea and ischaemic heart disease is booked for gastroscopy and colonoscopy. Discuss the perioperative considerations, including sedation versus general anaesthesia.
items.a:
## Preop

**Obstructive sleep apnoea**
- Sedation causes upper airway collapse, desaturation and hypoventilation; STOP-Bang screening and CPAP use matter (BJA). If he uses CPAP, bring it and use it afterwards; those who cannot tolerate CPAP need HDU after general anaesthesia.
- Opioids and benzodiazepines are particularly risky; avoid long-acting agents.

**Ischaemic heart disease**
- Avoid tachycardia, hypotension and hypertension; propofol sedation can reduce blood pressure, so titrate carefully. Continue beta blocker and aspirin; review recent ECG, functional capacity and the stent or infarct history.
- Bowel preparation causes dehydration and electrolyte disturbance (potassium and magnesium), which add to arrhythmia risk and hypotension on sedation.

**Combined procedures**
- A gastroscopy and colonoscopy under one anaesthetic are long; fasting for gastroscopy and bowel preparation for colonoscopy interact, and a patient with diabetes needs a glucose plan. The airway is shared with the endoscopist.
- Colonoscopy can cause vagal reactions, perforation (a surgical emergency) and bleeding.

## Intraop

The Blue Book decision framework is aspiration risk, airway protection and respiratory reserve. For this patient, reserve is limited by OSA, so I would involve a trained anaesthetist and use:
- **Monitoring:** ECG, saturation, non-invasive pressure and continuous **capnography**, with supplemental oxygen by nasal prongs or high-flow oxygen.
- **Sedation:** a targeted propofol infusion with a small dose of short-acting opioid, avoiding benzodiazepines, in the lateral position with a jaw thrust available and airway adjuncts and suction ready.
- Consider tracheal intubation for significant retention, inability to protect the airway or complex prolonged upper-GI intervention. Reassess or defer elective endoscopy if cardiac disease is unstable. OSA alone does not mandate general anaesthesia.

## Postop

Have a recovery plan: a head-up position, oxygen and CPAP, monitored until fully awake, and no discharge until safe. If a GLP-1 agonist is taken, follow the 2025 guidance (ask, do not stop routinely, 24 hour fluids or treat as a full stomach).

Agree intended sedation depth, staffing and a plan for unintentional deep sedation. Use capnography when indicated by depth and risk. Resume positive airway pressure when indicated, check readiness for discharge, and ensure the appropriate escort and written instructions if going home. Reassess the risks before giving additional doses or extending the procedure.

**Sources:** [ANZCA professional documents including PG09, PG07 and PG56](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/standards-of-practice/professional-documents) · [BJA Education anaesthesia and sedation for ERCP](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9482865/)

## Self-marking checklist

- OSA screening, CPAP and avoidance of long-acting sedatives
- Ischaemic heart disease: haemodynamic goals and medication
- Effects of bowel preparation: dehydration and electrolytes
- Combined procedures, vagal reactions and perforation risk
- Decision framework: aspiration, airway protection and respiratory reserve
- Monitoring with capnography and a titrated propofol technique
- Indications for general anaesthesia instead of sedation
- Recovery, CPAP and GLP-1 agonist guidance

items.title: 13. Ulcerative colitis on infliximab for colectomy
items.q: A 32-year-old with ulcerative colitis on infliximab and prednisolone needs emergency subtotal colectomy and ileostomy. Discuss the perioperative considerations.
items.a:
## Disease and presentation

Ulcerative colitis is restricted to the colon and rectum, with mucosal inflammation. Crohn's disease can affect any part of the gut with transmural disease, fistulae, strictures and malnutrition. Surgery is needed for acute severe colitis unresponsive to medical therapy (about 7 days of intravenous steroids and rescue ciclosporin or infliximab), **toxic megacolon**, perforation, haemorrhage, obstruction and dysplasia.

## Problems

- **Hypovolaemia and electrolyte disorders:** diarrhoea, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, metabolic acidosis (bicarbonate loss).
- **Sepsis and inflammation,** and anaemia (iron deficiency, chronic disease).
- **Malnutrition and hypoalbuminaemia,** which raise the risk of anastomotic leak and wound infection.
- **Venous thromboembolism:** inflammatory bowel disease is a prothrombotic state, so give pharmacological prophylaxis unless bleeding.
- **Steroids:** adrenal suppression needs cover with hydrocortisone (100 mg at induction, then 200 mg per 24 hours).
- **Immunosuppressants:** infliximab and other biologics raise infection risk (and delay healing), azathioprine can cause marrow suppression.
- Extraintestinal disease: primary sclerosing cholangitis, ankylosing spondylitis (neck and airway), arthritis.

## Preop

Resuscitate and correct fluids, potassium and magnesium; transfuse if needed; start antibiotics and consider stopping or delaying biologics according to the gastroenterologist. Assess nutrition, check coagulation and group and screen. Arrange stoma counselling and marking where time allows.

## Intraop

- **1.** **Rapid sequence induction** (emergency, possible ileus, full stomach), arterial line and large-bore access, central access if shocked.
- **2.** Cautious induction in a hypovolaemic patient, with noradrenaline early.
- **3.** Goal-directed fluids with balanced crystalloid; avoid excess saline (hyperchloraemic acidosis) and avoid oedema of the anastomosis.
- **4.** Maintain normothermia and lung-protective ventilation. Give antibiotics appropriate to surgery and infection, with redosing by protocol. Use blood products when indicated and manage haemostasis according to clinical bleeding.
- **5.** Analgesia: multimodal, with epidural or transversus abdominis plane or rectus sheath blocks; **avoid NSAIDs**, which can flare colitis.

## Postop

Stoma output monitoring, high output management (fluid, loperamide), early feeding, thromboprophylaxis, and surveillance for leak, ileus and infection. ERAS principles apply where the patient is fit.

Agree urgency and distinguish toxic megacolon, perforation and severe refractory colitis. Review steroid duration and suppression risk, active infection, recent biologic exposure, anaemia, malnutrition and VTE. Do not delay source control for a biologic washout. Plan to reassess steroid cover and taper with surgery and gastroenterology. During recovery document urine and stoma output, sodium, potassium and magnesium, and distinguish expected ileostomy losses from sepsis or an intra-abdominal complication.

**Sources:** [ERAS Society elective colorectal surgery recommendations 2025](https://www.erassociety.org/guidelines/) · [ERAS Society emergency laparotomy Part 2](https://www.erassociety.org/guideline/consensus-guidelines-for-perioperative-care-for-emergency-laparotomy-enhanced-recovery-after-surgery-eras-society-recommendations-part-2-emergency-laparotomy-intra-and-postoperative/) · [ESPEN surgical nutrition update 2025](https://www.clinicalnutritionjournal.com/article/S0261-5614%2825%2900243-2/fulltext)

## Self-marking checklist

- Crohn's disease versus ulcerative colitis
- Indications for emergency surgery
- Fluid, electrolyte and nutritional problems
- Venous thromboembolism risk
- Steroid and biologic management
- Induction and fluid strategy
- Analgesia and NSAID avoidance
- Stoma and postoperative care

items.title: 14. Severe COPD for laparoscopic cholecystectomy
items.q: A 68-year-old woman with severe COPD and ischaemic heart disease is booked for laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Discuss the perioperative considerations.
items.a:
## Risks

**Respiratory (FEV1 38%)**
- CO2 absorption and reduced diaphragm movement lead to hypercarbia and acidosis that a patient with severe COPD cannot compensate for; air trapping rises with higher minute ventilation.
- Elevated airway pressures and risk of barotrauma (bullae, pneumothorax), atelectasis, and V/Q mismatch. Postoperative pulmonary complications are likely.

**Cardiac (ischaemic heart disease)**
- Pneumoperitoneum raises afterload and heart rate and lowers venous return and cardiac output; hypercarbia causes tachycardia and hypertension. The mismatch can cause ischaemia.
- Vagal bradycardia on insufflation and the position changes (reverse Trendelenburg for cholecystectomy lowers preload).

**Other:** gas embolism, pneumothorax, subcutaneous emphysema, and the potential to convert to an open procedure.

BJA Education states the patient's ability to tolerate a potentially prolonged pneumoperitoneum with CO2 must be considered, particularly with coexisting cardiac or respiratory dysfunction.

## Preop

Discuss indication and whether the patient is at respiratory or cardiac baseline. Optimise bronchodilators and consider deferring elective surgery for an exacerbation or unstable cardiac symptoms. Assess functional capacity and obtain targeted ECG, gas or echo when results will change management. Discuss working pressure and conversion with surgery.

## Intraop

- **Monitoring:** arterial line with blood gases, capnography, airway pressures, ECG with ST analysis, and temperature.
- **Insufflation:** a low pressure of 8 to 10 mmHg, slow, with a steep tilt avoided; atropine ready.
- **Ventilation:** controlled ventilation with a low tidal volume (6 to 8 mL/kg), a long expiratory time to avoid dynamic hyperinflation, minimal PEEP and acceptance of moderate hypercapnia (target a pH above about 7.25 rather than a normal PaCO2). Peak pressures should be checked and reversible causes treated (BJA bariatric).
- **Circulation:** avoid tachycardia, hypotension and hypertension; use a titrated vasopressor and a cautious volume.
- **Drugs:** avoid nitrous oxide; short-acting agents; full reversal of neuromuscular block.
- **Recognise complications:** pneumothorax and gas embolism (Blue Book steps).

## Postop

extubate awake and sitting, give multimodal analgesia with local infiltration, avoid excess opioid, use CPAP or non-invasive ventilation, chest physiotherapy, and HDU monitoring including troponin if clinically suspected.

Check expiratory flow returns to baseline before the next breath. If hypotension and high pressures suggest gas trapping, temporarily release positive pressure as appropriate while checking alternative causes. Plan postoperative NIV according to baseline physiology and recovery.

**Sources:** [BJA Education minimally invasive abdominal and pelvic surgery](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2019.04.001) · [ANZCA professional documents including PG09, PG07 and PG56](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/standards-of-practice/professional-documents)

## Self-marking checklist

- Respiratory risks: hypercarbia, air trapping, barotrauma
- Cardiac risks: afterload, heart rate, venous return and position
- Choice of approach and alternatives to laparoscopy
- Preoperative optimisation and testing
- Low insufflation pressure and slow insufflation with atropine ready
- COPD ventilation strategy with permissive hypercapnia
- Avoid nitrous oxide; detect embolism and pneumothorax
- Postoperative HDU, NIV and analgesia

items.title: 15. Pelvic exenteration after previous irradiation
items.q: A patient with previously irradiated recurrent rectal cancer is scheduled for pelvic exenteration. Discuss the perioperative considerations, including haemorrhage and postoperative support.
items.a:
## Preop

Review the multidisciplinary plan, intended extent of resection, vascular involvement and possible rectal, urinary or flap reconstruction. Review prior radiotherapy and surgery, which can make dissection and bleeding control difficult. Assess frailty, exercise capacity, nutrition, anaemia, renal reserve and previous oncological treatment. Discuss blood products, expected analgesia, previous opioid exposure, stoma care, recovery and likely critical care needs. Optimise treatable deficits within the oncologic timetable and consider prehabilitation where feasible. Plan antibiotics, VTE prevention and the implications of antithrombotics for regional analgesia. Agree contingency plans for severe haemorrhage, prolonged positioning and damage control.

## Intraop

Arrange sufficient trained support and access for a long procedure with limited access to the patient after positioning or draping. Use arterial monitoring and reliable large-bore access if anticipated bleeding warrants it. Anticipate presacral venous or iliac vessel bleeding. Coordinate rapid transfusion and source control with the surgical team. Track gas, haemoglobin, calcium, temperature and coagulation, and use blood or haemostatic products guided by clinical bleeding and local protocol. Use balanced fluid and vasoactive support according to physiology. Avoid allowing sustained hypotension or avoidable volume excess. When haemostasis is achieved, reassess perfusion and replacement needs.

Use careful lithotomy positioning. Pad pressure points, avoid excessive joint excursion and agree planned leg and position checks, because prolonged elevation and hypoperfusion can contribute to well-leg compartment syndrome. Use lung-protective ventilation, active warming, antibiotic redosing and quantitative neuromuscular monitoring. Choose procedure-specific multimodal analgesia. Consider epidural benefit and its limitations if coagulopathy or hypotension is likely. Have a systemic or abdominal wall alternative. Coordinate local anaesthetic exposure and anticipate pain from multiple operative sites.

## Postop

Choose a monitored destination according to physiological course, haemorrhage, reconstruction and respiratory support. Handover drains, bowel and urinary anatomy, any flap surveillance and thresholds for surgery review. Assess early haemorrhage, sepsis, intra-abdominal collection, enteric or urinary leak, AKI and limb compartment syndrome. Check new disproportionate calf pain or motor deficit promptly, particularly if epidural analgesia obscures symptoms. Regularly review perfusion, fluid balance, stoma or urinary losses and electrolytes. Provide analgesia, VTE prophylaxis, individualised feeding and mobilisation. Arrange stoma and rehabilitation support and communicate plans for any staged operation with the patient and team.

**Sources:** [PelvEx Collaborative anaesthetic and perioperative consensus](https://pure.eur.nl/ws/portalfiles/portal/95920073/Perioperative_management_and_anaesthetic_considerations_in_pelvic_exenterations_using_Delphi_methodology_results_from_the_PelvEx_Collaborative.pdf) · [ERAS Society elective colorectal surgery recommendations 2025](https://www.erassociety.org/guidelines/) · [ESPEN surgical nutrition update 2025](https://www.clinicalnutritionjournal.com/article/S0261-5614%2825%2900243-2/fulltext)

## Self-marking checklist

- Recognises radiation, operative extent and recovery implications
- Plans equipment, access, monitoring and staffing
- Anticipates severe haemorrhage and describes physiology-guided replacement
- Prevents and recognises positioning injury
- Individualises analgesia and regional safety
- Monitors reconstructed organs, perfusion and complications

items.title: 16. Sleeve gastrectomy at BMI 52
items.q: A 42-year-old woman with BMI 52 kg/m² and obstructive sleep apnoea on CPAP is booked for laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy. Discuss the perioperative considerations.
items.a:
## Preop

- **Airway and OSA:** screen with STOP-Bang; she is already on CPAP and should bring the machine for use afterwards. Without tolerance of CPAP she needs HDU. Assess neck circumference and Mallampati, as BMI alone adds only a small intubation risk (BJA). NAP4 found obesity raised the risk of airway obstruction and regurgitation, particularly at extubation.
- **Risk:** the OS-MRS score; 4 to 5 points means HDU or ICU admission (BJA). Look for hypoventilation (bicarbonate), pulmonary hypertension (echo), diabetes, hypertension and ischaemic disease; ECG is essential.
- **Drugs:** she may be on a two to four week 800 kcal "liver shrinkage" diet (reduces liver volume by 16 to 20%, BJA). Stop an SGLT2 inhibitor at least 2 days before to avoid euglycaemic ketoacidosis (Blue Book 2019, ketones above 0.6 mmol/L). A GLP-1 agonist slows gastric emptying, so follow the 2025 guidance: ask, do not routinely stop, use a 24 hour clear fluid diet or treat as a full stomach.

## Intraop

- **Equipment and positioning:** a table rated for her weight, self-transfer onto the table, reverse Trendelenburg and a ramped head position, two cannulae.
- **Airway:** preoxygenate with a tight mask, ramped, to an end-tidal oxygen of 90%; CPAP or high-flow oxygen can help; use a video laryngoscope and a tracheal tube (BJA).
- Use drug-specific weight scalars, local dosing guidance and titration to observed effect. Ventilate using predicted body weight, titrate induction to effect and use quantitative neuromuscular monitoring with an appropriate reversal plan.
- **Ventilation:** 6 to 8 mL/kg of ideal weight and PEEP 5 to 10.
- **Neuromuscular block:** rocuronium with quantitative monitoring and full reversal with sugammadex.
- **Orogastric tube:** the surgeon may ask for a 34 Fr bougie or methylene blue (60 to 180 mL); pass it by the oral route and remove any gastric tube, because it can be stapled (BJA).
- **Analgesia and PONV:** multimodal and opioid-sparing, with local infiltration, ketamine, clonidine and NSAIDs; TIVA and two or three antiemetics (BJA).

## Postop

Extubate fully awake and sitting up. Monitor for a **leak** (0.8 to 1.5%; a persistent tachycardia is a leak until proved otherwise, BJA), bleeding (0.5 to 4%), VTE (mechanical plus drug prophylaxis) and hypoventilation, using CPAP. Use ERAS: early mobilisation and a staged dietitian plan. Blue Book 2019 notes ketoacidosis may occur up to 5 to 6 weeks after surgery.

Check GLP-1/GIP and SGLT2 use separately. Apply the ANZCA clear-fluid pathway for GLP-1/GIP and the local fasting and ketosis pathway for SGLT2 inhibitors. Screening for obesity hypoventilation and the need for postoperative PAP can change the destination.

**Sources:** [BJA Education anaesthesia for bariatric surgery](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2021.12.007) · [ANZCA GLP-1 and GLP-1/GIP recommendations](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/standards-of-practice/clinical-practice-recommendations-regarding-patients-taking-glp-1) · [SOBA airway recommendations 2025](https://doi.org/10.1111/anae.16647)

## Self-marking checklist

- OSA screening, CPAP and OS-MRS risk score with HDU criteria
- Preoperative diet, SGLT2 inhibitor and GLP-1 agonist management
- Ramped positioning, preoxygenation to EtO2 90%, video laryngoscope
- Weight scalars for lean, adjusted and total body weight
- Lung-protective ventilation with peak pressure tolerance
- Rocuronium with quantitative monitoring; orogastric tube and methylene blue precautions
- Opioid-sparing multimodal analgesia, TIVA and PONV prophylaxis
- Postoperative leak, bleeding, VTE and OSA monitoring

items.title: 17. Ivor Lewis oesophagectomy: intraoperative management
items.q: Discuss the intraoperative anaesthetic management of a patient undergoing a two-stage (Ivor Lewis) oesophagectomy.
items.a:
## Plan and set-up

An Ivor Lewis oesophagectomy has an abdominal phase (supine, laparotomy or laparoscopy, gastric mobilisation, jejunostomy) and a right thoracic phase (left lateral, one-lung ventilation of the right lung, anastomosis). Epidural or paravertebral analgesia is planned, and ICU care is booked.

## Intraoperative management

- **Monitoring and access:** arterial line (pre-induction), central line, two large cannulae, temperature, urine output and a cardiac output monitor where available.
- **Airway:** rapid sequence induction if there is dysphagia, obstruction or reflux (a full stomach), then a left double-lumen tube or bronchial blocker, confirmed bronchoscopically and rechecked after turning.
- **Analgesia:** a thoracic epidural or paravertebral catheter placed before incision, with intrathecal morphine, a wound catheter or a trunk block as alternatives (BJA reports no survival or pain difference between epidural and PCA in pancreatic surgery, and epidurals cause hypotension).
- **One-lung ventilation:** tidal volume 4 to 6 mL/kg, PEEP 5 and FiO2 titrated; limit plateau pressure, and use an alveolar recruitment manoeuvre before re-expansion. If hypoxia develops, confirm the tube position, give 100% oxygen, add CPAP to the non-ventilated lung, and add PEEP to the ventilated lung, then clip the pulmonary artery as a last resort. Permissive hypercapnia is acceptable.
- **Haemodynamics:** hypotension from mediastinal and caval compression during mobilisation, arrhythmia (atrial fibrillation in up to 20% from memory), and bleeding. Maintain MAP with vasopressors and avoid excess fluid (restrictive, balanced crystalloid), because oedema impairs the anastomosis and the lungs (BJA).
- **Gastric conduit perfusion:** promptly treat sustained hypotension and assess flow, intravascular volume and bleeding. A titrated vasopressor can restore perfusion after assessment. Avoid repeated empirical fluid boluses and check possible surgical causes.
- **Temperature and positioning:** warm the patient, pad the dependent arm and the axilla, and protect the eyes and brachial plexus.
- **Tubes:** do not insert a nasogastric tube blind once the stomach is divided; the surgeon places it. (The bariatric article warns of stapling a tube.)
- **Antibiotics, PONV and VTE prophylaxis** as for major abdominal surgery.

## Emergence

Aim for extubation at the end if the patient is warm, awake, comfortable and not hypoxic, because positive pressure ventilation can stress the anastomosis; otherwise ventilate in ICU. Keep the patient upright, give early physiotherapy, and watch for anastomotic leak, pneumonia and arrhythmia.

**Sources:** [ERAS Society oesophagectomy guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30276441/) · [ESPEN surgical nutrition update 2025](https://www.clinicalnutritionjournal.com/article/S0261-5614%2825%2900243-2/fulltext)

## Self-marking checklist

- Set-up for abdominal and thoracic phases with analgesia plan
- Monitoring including arterial line and central access
- Rapid sequence induction and double-lumen tube checks
- One-lung ventilation settings and hypoxia algorithm
- Haemodynamic problems from mediastinal manipulation and fluid restriction
- Gastric conduit perfusion and avoidance of blind nasogastric tubes
- Warming, positioning and nerve protection
- Extubation criteria and postoperative complications

items.title: 18. Whipple procedure with obstructive jaundice
items.q: A 64-year-old man with a pancreatic head tumour and obstructive jaundice is scheduled for pancreaticoduodenectomy. Discuss the perioperative considerations.
items.a:
## Preop

- **Risk:** morbidity up to 50%. The NSQIP risk factors are age over 74, ASA above 2, BMI above 40, preoperative sepsis, dependent status, coronary disease, dyspnoea, bleeding disorder and proximal resection (BJA). CPET: an anaerobic threshold below 10 predicts a longer stay and pancreatic leak.
- **Cancer effects:** cachexia (up to 80%), anaemia (give IV iron if surgery is within 6 weeks), sarcopenia and nutrition (protein 1.5 g/kg/day, MUST or NRS-2002).
- **Jaundice:** haemodynamic instability, acute kidney injury, myocardial depression, coagulopathy, immunosuppression and poor healing. ERAS advises avoiding preoperative biliary drainage unless the bilirubin is above 250 μmol/L; routine stenting does not reduce mortality (BJA). Give IV vitamin K, and do not give plasma for the INR alone (Blue Book).
- **Gastric outlet obstruction:** rapid sequence induction as for a full stomach (BJA).
- **Other:** diabetes (HbA1c, insulin infusion), smoking for at least 4 weeks, alcohol withdrawal prophylaxis, and prehabilitation for 3 to 6 weeks.

## Intraop

- **Monitoring and access:** arterial line, large-bore access and a central line; a cardiac output monitor is optional, because it has not reduced complications (BJA).
- **Haemodynamics:** MAP above 65. IVC compression, portal and SMV manipulation reduce venous return, and bleeding can be sudden and concealed, so communicate with the surgeon. Vein resection risks hepatic ischaemia.
- **Fluids:** a restrictive approach protects the pancreaticojejunostomy, but a highly positive balance (over 6.8 L at 48 hours) is associated with complications and may simply reflect the inflammatory response; use balanced crystalloid and vasopressors.
- **Analgesia:** epidural analgesia is still ERAS-recommended, but the PAKMAN trial found no difference in survival or pain compared with PCA, and epidurals fail and cause hypotension and vasopressor use; alternatives are intrathecal morphine, wound infusion and a multimodal opioid-sparing plan (BJA).
- **Prolonged surgery:** antibiotics redosed, VTE prophylaxis (4 weeks for cancer), normothermia and pressure care.
- **Somatostatin analogues** are not recommended routinely (BJA).

## Postop

Select ward, HDU or ICU by physiological risk, resection extent and actual organ-support needs. Monitor glucose (total pancreatectomy gives brittle diabetes and needs an insulin infusion). Watch for a pancreatic fistula (clinically relevant drain output on or after day 3 with amylase above three times the institutional upper normal serum value), haemorrhage (early within 24 to 48 hours, late at 1 to 3 weeks from a leak or pseudoaneurysm), delayed gastric emptying (the leading morbidity, erythromycin helps), and respiratory failure on days 3 to 7. ERAS: early drain removal at 72 hours, no routine nasogastric tube, early mobilisation.

**Sources:** [BJA Education pancreatic resection Part 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11785549/) · [BJA Education pancreatic resection Part 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12190887/) · [ESPEN surgical nutrition update 2025](https://www.clinicalnutritionjournal.com/article/S0261-5614%2825%2900243-2/fulltext)

## Self-marking checklist

- Risk factors and CPET threshold
- Jaundice effects and ERAS biliary drainage threshold (bilirubin above 250)
- Cachexia, anaemia and nutrition with specific targets
- Gastric outlet obstruction as a full stomach
- Haemodynamic plan including IVC compression and bleeding
- Restrictive fluids with MAP above 65
- Analgesia choices with PAKMAN evidence
- Postoperative fistula, haemorrhage, delayed gastric emptying and glycaemia

items.title: 19. Right hemihepatectomy: intraoperative management
items.q: Discuss the intraoperative anaesthetic management of a patient undergoing a right hemihepatectomy for colorectal liver metastases.
items.a:
## Preoperative points that shape the intraoperative plan

Colorectal metastases are the main indication. Know the future liver remnant (at least 20% in a normal liver, 30 to 40% after hepatotoxic chemotherapy or with steatohepatitis, and at least 50% in cirrhosis), whether portal vein embolisation was used, and when chemotherapy finished (delay 4 to 6 weeks).

## Intraoperative management

- **Monitoring and access:** large-bore access, an arterial line, and a central line (CVP is unreliable under pneumoperitoneum, so many centres omit it for laparoscopic cases); cardiac output monitoring, temperature, and blood and products ready.
- **Technique:** general anaesthesia with a tracheal tube, agents with minimal effect on liver blood flow, short-acting drugs for a clear-headed emergence (BJA).
- **Transection phase:** coordinate a temporary low hepatic venous pressure period when appropriate. ERAS cites a CVP below 5 cm H₂O with close monitoring in selected cases. Individualise to perfusion and bleeding. Restore effective circulating volume after transection, and abandon a low-CVP plan when shock or significant end-organ hypoperfusion develops.
- **Inflow occlusion (Pringle):** clamping the hepatoduodenal ligament lowers venous return and raises SVR with haemodynamic instability, so communicate with the surgeon. It is used intermittently (10 to 20 minutes on and 5 off) because prolonged occlusion (over 1 hour in a normal liver, 30 minutes in a diseased liver) causes ischaemia-reperfusion injury. **Total vascular exclusion** adds IVC clamping and causes profound haemodynamic change.
- **Blood loss:** it can be sudden, and the CUSA suction canister can hide it under the drapes; check regularly. Use tranexamic acid, cell salvage where appropriate, avoid hypothermia, and treat coagulopathy using viscoelastic testing rather than the INR.
- **Analgesia:** thoracic epidural is not recommended by ERAS; use intrathecal morphine, wound catheters or abdominal wall blocks, with paracetamol and NSAIDs (BJA).
- **Other:** balanced crystalloid, normothermia and glucose control.

## Laparoscopic or robotic resection

Pneumoperitoneum has a tamponade effect that reduces venous bleeding, but CO2 tolerance matters in patients with cardiorespiratory disease, and conversion occurs in up to 20% (BJA).

## Postop

HDU or ICU for major resections. Watch for post-hepatectomy liver failure (an increasing INR and bilirubin from day 5, 8 to 12%), bile leak, haemorrhage and renal dysfunction; avoid nephrotoxins and hepatotoxic drugs.

**Sources:** [BJA Education perioperative management for hepatic resection](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2022.05.002) · [ERAS Society recommendations for liver surgery](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00268-022-06732-5)

## Self-marking checklist

- Future liver remnant thresholds and chemotherapy timing
- Monitoring plan and CVP caveat with pneumoperitoneum
- Low CVP strategy with evidence and risks
- Pringle and total vascular exclusion haemodynamics
- Blood loss recognition, tranexamic acid and viscoelastic testing
- Analgesia alternatives to epidural
- Laparoscopic resection considerations
- Postoperative liver failure monitoring

items.title: 20. Major liver trauma and damage-control laparotomy
items.q: A patient with a high-grade liver injury remains in shock and needs damage-control laparotomy. Discuss the perioperative considerations specific to major liver trauma.
items.a:
## Preop

Activate the trauma and major haemorrhage pathways, involve senior surgery, anaesthesia, transfusion and interventional radiology and arrange ICU. Resuscitate in parallel with preparation for haemorrhage control. Obtain rapid access, crossmatch and baseline gas, coagulation and ionised calcium when feasible. Assess for concurrent chest, head or pelvic injury and use physiological trajectory to determine urgency. An unstable patient with likely ongoing abdominal bleeding may need immediate laparotomy. A stable patient or selected responder may follow imaging and embolisation pathways. Document the plan for a potentially unstable induction and have blood, warming and appropriate airway equipment ready. Use an induction strategy matched to shock and aspiration risk and prepare for immediate deterioration.

## Intraop

Prioritise surgical haemorrhage control and physiological resuscitation. Use blood components guided by the major haemorrhage protocol and laboratory or viscoelastic results if available. Limit dilution, maintain temperature, monitor lactate, electrolytes and coagulation and correct clinically important hypocalcaemia. Coordinate early trauma tranexamic acid when indicated by the protocol and injury timing. Traumatic use differs from elective oncological hepatectomy prophylaxis. Agree adequate perfusion goals, particularly if traumatic brain injury coexists.

Understand what the surgeon is testing. Packing and compression can tamponade bleeding. A Pringle manoeuvre occludes hepatic arterial and portal venous inflow. Bleeding that persists despite effective inflow occlusion raises concern for hepatic vein or retrohepatic caval injury or another source. Do not pursue elective low-CVP goals during uncontrolled shock. Anticipate instability during clamp or pack release, with possible recurrent bleeding, acidaemia and electrolyte disturbances. Communicate before each release and be ready to provide immediate support. Damage-control surgery may use temporary closure, with definitive repair once physiology improves.

## Postop

Handover actual and suspected sources, packing, clamp duration, transfusion, remaining injuries and reintervention timing. Monitor perfusion, gas, urine output, hepatic function, coagulation and abdominal pressure when indicated. Reassess for abdominal compartment syndrome, recurrent haemorrhage and hypoperfusion. Later complications include bile leak, biloma, infection, biliary injury and liver failure. Coordinate ICU optimisation, reassessment for embolisation and planned re-look. Agree when to restart VTE prophylaxis once haemostasis and injury pattern permit, and document the plan for ongoing organ support.

Avoid treating a reassuring early haemoglobin as evidence that bleeding has stopped.

**Sources:** [BJA Education anaesthesia for abdominal trauma](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2024.09.005) · [BJA Education perioperative management for hepatic resection](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2022.05.002)

## Self-marking checklist

- Triggers major haemorrhage and urgent source control
- Individualises induction to shock and associated injuries
- Uses trauma-specific blood component and physiological support
- Distinguishes Pringle inflow from venous or caval bleeding
- Anticipates clamp release and avoids elective low-CVP targets
- Plans ICU surveillance and return for definitive care

items.title: 21. DIEP free-flap breast reconstruction
items.q: A patient is scheduled for immediate DIEP free-flap breast reconstruction after mastectomy. Discuss the perioperative considerations, including flap perfusion and analgesia.
items.a:
## Preop

Clarify the mastectomy, laterality, expected duration, donor-site surgery, prior abdominal scars and flap-monitoring plan. Review frailty, active cancer therapies and cardiotoxic exposure, nutrition, anaemia, diabetes, smoking and prior radiotherapy. Identify anticipated access and positioning constraints. Agree a VTE plan with the team, accounting for prolonged surgery, cancer, bleeding risk and regional techniques. Explain the need for postoperative flap surveillance and possible urgent return to theatre. Plan analgesia for both chest and abdominal donor sites, taking account of patient preference and resources. Assess PONV risk and preoperative functional support.

## Intraop

Use a secured airway and reliable vascular access. Consider arterial monitoring for long or complex procedures according to reserve. Maintain normothermia, adequate oxygenation and sufficient systemic perfusion. Replace losses based on the clinical trajectory and avoid repeated empirical fluid boluses for all hypotension. Excess fluid can promote oedema and impair venous drainage. Titrate vasopressors where appropriate after evaluating volume, bleeding and anaesthetic depth. Discuss the target with the surgeon and reassess after reperfusion. Address unexpected flap deterioration by checking systemic factors and promptly requesting surgical assessment for kinking, compression, arterial insufficiency or venous thrombosis. Position and pad carefully, protect nerves and avoid inaccessible or compressive monitoring arrangements.

Use multimodal analgesia, such as paracetamol and a suitable NSAID depending on bleeding and renal risk. Add an appropriate chest-wall technique and donor-site infiltration or abdominal wall block when indicated. Coordinate local anaesthetic dose between teams and use short-acting opioid rescue. Provide antiemetic prophylaxis and active warming. Consider surgical duration and haemodynamics when choosing the recovery destination.

## Postop

Hand over the flap-specific monitoring method, expected Doppler signal and thresholds for immediate surgical review. Monitor colour, temperature, capillary refill, turgor and Doppler as specified. Unexplained flap discolouration, venous congestion or signal loss requires prompt assessment and potential exploration. Maintain adequate perfusion, oxygenation, analgesia and temperature while checking for bleeding and haematoma. Mobilise with appropriate positioning and implement the agreed VTE plan. Assess both surgical sites, manage nausea and restart nutrition as safe. Coordinate follow-up with plastic and breast teams and discuss functional recovery with the patient.

Confirm that the monitoring plan and emergency contact are understood by the receiving ward.

**Sources:** [ERAS Society breast reconstruction recommendations](https://erassociety.org/guidelines/?speciality=breast) · [ESPEN surgical nutrition update 2025](https://www.clinicalnutritionjournal.com/article/S0261-5614%2825%2900243-2/fulltext)

## Self-marking checklist

- Plans patient and procedure-specific risk assessment
- Explains systemic perfusion and flap-specific causes
- Avoids fluid overload while using appropriate vasoactive support
- Covers both surgical sites for analgesia
- Specifies flap surveillance and urgent escalation
- Plans recovery, VTE measures and multidisciplinary handover

items.title: 22. Anatomy after Roux-en-Y bypass and oesophagectomy
items.q: Describe the anatomical changes after a Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and an oesophagectomy, and the implications for later anaesthesia.
items.a:
## Roux-en-Y gastric bypass

**Anatomy:** the stomach is divided to make a small upper pouch that is anastomosed to a Roux limb of jejunum, so food bypasses the distal stomach, the duodenum and the proximal jejunum; a distal jejunojejunal anastomosis delivers the digestive juices (BJA).

**Implications**
- **Aspiration and the excluded stomach:** the pouch can still hold food and cause obstruction or dumping symptoms, while the excluded gastric remnant cannot be reached by an ordinary nasogastric tube and can distend in an obstruction.
- **Tubes and devices:** a blind nasogastric tube may perforate the pouch or anastomosis; it should be placed under direct guidance and be avoided in the early period.
- **Acute abdomen:** consider an **internal hernia** (a late, difficult diagnosis through mesenteric defects), anastomotic leak, stricture, bleeding (staple line; BJA), and marginal ulcer.
- **Nutrition and drugs:** deficiencies of iron, B12, folate, calcium and vitamin D need lifelong supplements; check the full blood count and micronutrients. Altered absorption may change oral drug uptake.
- **Metabolic:** dumping syndrome (pain, flushing, diarrhoea); hypoglycaemia; ketoacidosis may occur up to 5 to 6 weeks after surgery in patients on SGLT2 inhibitors (Blue Book 2019).

**Sleeve gastrectomy and gastric band:** sleeve gastrectomy leaves a banana-shaped stomach and may worsen reflux (BJA); band slippage causes vomiting and pain, and erosion is a rare emergency.

## Oesophagectomy

**Anatomy:** the oesophagus is removed and replaced by a gastric tube (conduit) pulled into the chest and anastomosed in the chest or neck; a feeding jejunostomy is often present. The pylorus is drained or dilated.

**Implications**
- **High aspiration risk:** the sphincter is gone, the conduit empties slowly; a rapid sequence induction with a head-up position is needed, even after long fasts. Patients are often advised to sleep upright.
- **Respiratory:** reduced lung capacity, a conduit that compresses the lung, recurrent laryngeal injury, and chronic aspiration.
- **Tubes and devices:** a nasogastric tube must not be passed blindly; use endoscopic guidance because the anastomosis can be perforated.
- **Nutrition:** weight loss, vitamin B12 deficiency and dumping.
- **Extubation:** head-up and fully awake.
- **Anastomotic stricture** or leak can present with dysphagia or sepsis.

Find the operation note and ask the surgeon before any upper gastrointestinal procedure.

**Sources:** [BJA Education anaesthesia for bariatric surgery](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2021.12.007) · [ERAS Society oesophagectomy guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30276441/) · [ANZCA GLP-1 and GLP-1/GIP recommendations](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/standards-of-practice/clinical-practice-recommendations-regarding-patients-taking-glp-1)

## Self-marking checklist

- Roux-en-Y anatomy and why a pouch changes aspiration and tube risks
- Acute abdomen after bypass: internal hernia, leak, bleeding, marginal ulcer
- Nutritional deficiencies and drug absorption
- Dumping, hypoglycaemia and delayed ketoacidosis on SGLT2 inhibitors
- Sleeve gastrectomy and gastric band complications
- Oesophagectomy anatomy with conduit and aspiration risk
- Avoid blind nasogastric tubes after either operation
- Obtain the operation note and tailor the induction plan

items.title: 23. Severe gallstone pancreatitis
items.q: A 48-year-old man with acute severe pancreatitis from gallstones is admitted with respiratory distress. Outline the diagnosis, assessment of severity and management.
items.a:
## Diagnosis

Acute pancreatitis is diagnosed when two of three are present: typical epigastric pain radiating to the back, serum lipase or amylase above three times the upper limit of normal, and characteristic imaging. In a gallstone case, look for biliary obstruction (jaundice, raised bilirubin and ALT above about 150) and cholangitis (Charcot's triad).

Respiratory distress suggests a pancreatitis-associated lung injury: ARDS, a sympathetic pleural effusion, atelectasis from splinting, or aspiration.

## Severity (revised Atlanta, from memory)

- **Mild:** no organ failure.
- **Moderately severe:** transient organ failure (under 48 hours) or local complications.
- **Severe:** persistent organ failure (over 48 hours), assessed with the modified Marshall score (respiratory, renal and cardiovascular). Other aids are BISAP, APACHE II, CRP (above about 150 at 48 hours) and a high urea or haematocrit.

## Management

- **1.** **Early assessment and ICU or HDU** for organ failure, with an arterial line and urine output.
- **2.** **Respiratory:** oxygen, high-flow nasal oxygen or CPAP, and intubation with lung-protective ventilation for ARDS; watch for abdominal compartment syndrome.
- **3.** **Fluids:** early, goal-directed, moderate volumes of a balanced crystalloid (Ringer's lactate), reassessed frequently; aggressive fluid is associated with more fluid overload and respiratory failure.
- **4.** **Analgesia:** multimodal, with opioids as needed (fentanyl or hydromorphone), and epidural for severe pain once coagulation and sepsis allow.
- **5.** **Nutrition:** early enteral feeding within 24 to 72 hours, nasogastric or nasojejunal; parenteral only if enteral fails.
- **6.** **Biliary:** request early ERCP for cholangitis. Persistent duct obstruction requires specialist assessment. Avoid routine early ERCP in uncomplicated biliary pancreatitis without cholangitis. For mild biliary disease arrange same-admission cholecystectomy where appropriate.
- **7.** **Antibiotics:** not prophylactic; used for infected necrosis or cholangitis.
- **8.** **Complications:** necrosis (infected necrosis managed by delayed step-up drainage), pseudocyst, haemorrhage (pseudoaneurysm), venous thrombosis, hypocalcaemia and hyperglycaemia.
- **9.** Track creatinine, electrolytes including calcium, and glucose. Use renal replacement therapy for standard ICU indications and correct clinically important metabolic disturbances.

If the patient needs anaesthesia (drainage or ERCP), treat the airway as a full stomach.

Do not make a prediction of severity from the lipase concentration. Organ failure can evolve, so reassess after initial resuscitation and avoid routine early CT purely for severity. Use imaging earlier for diagnostic uncertainty, deterioration or suspected complications. WATERFALL found more fluid overload with aggressive fluid resuscitation without improved clinical outcomes in its study population. In a patient already in shock or respiratory failure, individualise support and monitoring.

**Sources:** [ACG acute pancreatitis guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38857482/) · [WATERFALL randomised trial](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2202884)

## Self-marking checklist

- Diagnostic criteria (two of three) and gallstone features
- Respiratory distress causes: ARDS, effusion, splinting
- Severity classification by organ failure duration
- ICU care with respiratory support
- Goal-directed balanced crystalloid fluids
- Multimodal analgesia
- Early enteral nutrition
- Urgent ERCP for cholangitis; complications and antibiotics

items.title: 24. ICU after mesenteric revascularisation
items.q: A patient returns to ICU after revascularisation and damage-control laparotomy for acute mesenteric ischaemia, with bowel viability uncertain. Outline your ICU management and thresholds for reintervention.
items.a:
## Understand the source-control plan

Clarify the cause, vascular procedure, length and segments of remaining bowel, viability concerns, residual contamination, abdominal closure, bowel continuity and planned second look. Discuss timing with general and vascular surgery. Confirm antithrombotic strategy by mechanism, revascularisation, bleeding and neuraxial constraints. Establish whether the patient is being treated for arterial embolism, thrombosis, venous thrombosis or a low-flow state. Review the preoperative trajectory and identify ongoing shock, haemorrhage or reperfusion risk. For an uncertain diagnosis or suspected reocclusion, urgent specialist review and CTA are appropriate when the findings will guide therapy. Serial lactate is useful only in context and a reassuring result does not exclude residual ischaemia.

## Support perfusion and manage organ injury

Use invasive monitoring where indicated and reassess dynamic response to balanced fluid or blood as appropriate. Use vasopressors when needed after evaluating preload, cardiac function and bleeding. Avoid indiscriminate fluid loading and sustained hypoperfusion. Track lactate, acid-base status, potassium, urine output, temperature, haemoglobin and coagulation. Reperfusion can produce vasodilation, hyperkalaemia and acidosis. Obtain ECG monitoring and treat severe electrolyte disturbances promptly under the ICU pathway. Use lung-protective ventilation and assess renal support when indicated. Give appropriate empiric antimicrobials for suspected contamination or sepsis and reassess after cultures and source-control findings.

Separate early expected instability from deterioration requiring action. Increasing pressor requirement, rising lactate, unexplained acidosis, new abdominal distension, bleeding, falling urine output or deteriorating respiratory mechanics prompt repeat examination and urgent senior review. Consider recurrent ischaemia, missed necrosis, bleeding, infection and abdominal compartment syndrome. Check bladder pressure if indicated. Do not treat the numbers alone if a reversible surgical cause is possible.

## Recovery and reintervention

Plan re-exploration, commonly within 24–48 hours when viability was uncertain, or earlier for deterioration. Document triggers and confirm who will act. Reassess the safety of enteral feeding according to perfusion, bowel continuity and the surgical plan. Avoid feeding into uncontrolled shock or suspected continuing ischaemia. Discuss early nutrition support as soon as feasible, with parenteral nutrition considered when prolonged enteral intolerance is expected. Replace stoma and gastric losses with ongoing electrolyte review. Plan sedation and analgesia, infection prevention, mobilisation and family communication, including the likely recovery trajectory and treatment goals.

**Sources:** [WSES acute mesenteric ischaemia guideline](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9580452/) · [ESVS mesenteric and renal vessels guideline 2025](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1078588425005167) · [ERAS Society emergency laparotomy Part 2](https://www.erassociety.org/guideline/consensus-guidelines-for-perioperative-care-for-emergency-laparotomy-enhanced-recovery-after-surgery-eras-society-recommendations-part-2-emergency-laparotomy-intra-and-postoperative/) · [ESPEN surgical nutrition update 2025](https://www.clinicalnutritionjournal.com/article/S0261-5614%2825%2900243-2/fulltext)

## Self-marking checklist

- Clarifies vascular cause, anatomy and source-control adequacy
- Sets physiological targets and recognises reperfusion
- Uses appropriate sepsis, ventilation and renal support
- Recognises deterioration and considers compartment syndrome
- Plans re-look with escalation triggers
- Addresses nutrition, losses, antithrombotics and multidisciplinary recovery

items.title: 25. Seizure from rapid hyponatraemia
items.q: Six hours after a major bowel resection a patient has a generalised seizure and a sodium concentration of 116 mmol/L. Outline your differential diagnosis, immediate treatment and how you would prevent overcorrection.
items.a:
## Immediate resuscitation

Call for senior and critical care help. Protect airway and ventilation, obtain monitoring and IV access, check bedside glucose and stop the seizure according to the emergency protocol. Assess recent opioids or local anaesthetic, oxygenation, hypotension, acute neurological events and other metabolic abnormalities. Severe symptoms with marked hyponatraemia are a medical emergency. Obtain a rapid repeat sodium and serum osmolality where practical but do not delay treatment when the association is plausible. Start bolus hypertonic saline according to the local emergency pathway. A commonly used regimen gives 100–150 mL of 3% saline per bolus with early reassessment. The initial goal is a modest rise of roughly 4–6 mmol/L to reduce cerebral oedema and improve symptoms, followed by reassessment. It is not immediate normalisation.

## Determine the cause

Review the preoperative sodium and time course, oral and IV intake, drug administration, renal function, fluid balance and losses. Pain, nausea, opioids and surgical stress promote non-osmotic vasopressin release. Hypotonic fluid or water excess may combine with impaired free-water excretion. Hypovolaemia from third-space, drain or GI losses, AKI, thiazides and adrenal insufficiency are alternatives. Assess volume status and measure glucose, renal function, potassium, serum osmolality and urine osmolality and sodium where results inform the mechanism. Interpret urine sodium in the context of diuretics and resuscitation. Consider hyperglycaemia-related or spurious low sodium separately and avoid attributing all postoperative confusion to sodium.

## Prevent overcorrection and recurrence

Use monitored care with serial sodium after boluses and frequently during active correction. Track urine output, because brisk water diuresis can rapidly raise sodium after volume replacement or reversal of the cause. Use conservative correction limits if duration is uncertain or osmotic demyelination risk is high, especially in malnutrition, hypokalaemia, liver disease or alcohol dependence. In high-risk patients aim well below an 8 mmol/L rise in 24 hours and consider potassium replacement in the correction calculation. Discuss desmopressin and free-water replacement or relowering with ICU or renal specialists if the sodium is rising too fast. Treat the underlying mechanism and review fluid prescribing, losses and the planned monitoring location. Hand over baseline sodium, given therapy, current trajectory and repeat testing time.

**Sources:** [European clinical guideline on hyponatraemia](https://academic.oup.com/ejendo/article/170/3/G1/6668028) · [ERAS Society emergency laparotomy Part 2](https://www.erassociety.org/guideline/consensus-guidelines-for-perioperative-care-for-emergency-laparotomy-enhanced-recovery-after-surgery-eras-society-recommendations-part-2-emergency-laparotomy-intra-and-postoperative/)

## Self-marking checklist

- Resuscitates and treats seizure and hypoglycaemia
- Recognises severe symptomatic hyponatraemia and uses hypertonic saline
- Targets early symptom control with modest rise
- Identifies postoperative mechanism and appropriate tests
- Monitors for brisk diuresis and limits correction
- Plans specialist response to overcorrection and handover

items.title: 26. Brain-dead organ donor
items.q: Describe the anaesthetic care of a brain-dead organ donor undergoing multi-organ procurement.
items.a:
## Principles

Brain-stem death is a legal death. The anaesthetist's role in a multi-organ retrieval is to maintain organ perfusion and protect the organs for the recipients; there is no need for anaesthesia for the donor's benefit, but the spinal reflexes and the sympathetic responses to incision require control.

## Physiology of brain death

- **Early:** an intense sympathetic surge (Cushing reflex, catecholamine storm) causes hypertension, tachycardia, arrhythmia, myocardial injury and neurogenic pulmonary oedema.
- **Late:** loss of sympathetic tone causes vasoplegia, hypotension and bradycardia; **diabetes insipidus** causes polyuria with hypernatraemia and hypovolaemia; there is hypothermia, coagulopathy and endocrine failure (thyroid, cortisol, insulin), plus a systemic inflammatory response.

## Anaesthetic management

**Monitoring and access:** arterial line, central line, urine output, temperature and cardiac output monitoring (echo or pulmonary artery catheter if needed), with blood gases.

**Targets:** agree organ-specific plans with retrieval and ICU teams. Aim for adequate perfusion, oxygenation, temperature and control of glucose, electrolytes and urine losses. Fixed CVP targets are not a measure of volume responsiveness.

**Components**
- **Cardiovascular:** euvolaemia with balanced crystalloid, and avoid overload (lung donation); vasopressin as first-line vasopressor (also treats diabetes insipidus), noradrenaline if needed, and dobutamine or adrenaline for low output.
- **Respiratory:** lung-protective ventilation (6 to 8 mL/kg, PEEP 8 to 10), recruitment, avoiding fluid overload; FiO2 titrated, and an apnoea test earlier, so a lung recruitment manoeuvre after disconnection.
- **Endocrine:** treat diabetes insipidus with desmopressin or vasopressin as appropriate, replace water and electrolytes carefully and use insulin if indicated. Discuss any steroid or thyroid therapy with the retrieval team. Avoid assuming a universal hormone replacement bundle.
- **Muscle relaxant and volatile or opioid:** spinal reflexes and hypertension and tachycardia on incision can occur, so use a neuromuscular blocker and a volatile agent or opioid as needed.
- **Temperature:** warm the patient, since hypothermia causes arrhythmia and coagulopathy.
- **Blood and coagulation:** transfuse to a haemoglobin of about 70 to 80 g/L; treat coagulopathy.
- **Heparin** before cross-clamp, and the preservation solution is given by the surgical team; stop ventilation when the lungs are clamped as instructed.

## Practical points

Communicate the order of organ removal and cross-clamp timing. Confirm the organ-specific medication and heparin plan with the retrieval team. Use the local protocol and be ready to manage sudden arrhythmias or arrest before cross-clamp.

Verify documentation of death and authorisation before transfer and separate retrieval decisions from the earlier independent determination of death. Expect spinal motor and haemodynamic responses and manage them respectfully. Confirm handover, preservation sequence and communication with the family through the coordinator.

**Sources:** [ANZICS Statement on Death and Organ Donation](https://www.anzics.org/advocacy/death-organ-donation-dodc/)

## Self-marking checklist

- Brain-stem death as legal death and the purpose of anaesthetic care
- Sympathetic surge followed by vasoplegia, diabetes insipidus, hypothermia and coagulopathy
- Monitoring and targets for MAP, CVP, urine output, sodium and temperature
- Vasopressin first-line with fluids and inotropes
- Lung-protective ventilation for lung donation
- Treats diabetes insipidus and individualises hormone therapy
- Spinal reflex control with neuromuscular blocker and volatile or opioid
- Warming, heparin and communication with retrieval team

items.title: 2025.1 Q13: Robotic surgery in steep head-down position
items.q: Describe the physiologic consequences and strategies for their mitigation in a patient undergoing prolonged robotic-assisted surgery in steep head-down position. (50%) Discuss the intraoperative considerations for a patient undergoing robotic surgery. (50%)
items.model:
## Physiological consequences and mitigation (50%)

The examiners rewarded each consequence linked to a specific mitigation; "limit the head-down time" alone earned nothing.

**Airway and breathing**
- Steep head-down with CO2 pneumoperitoneum (12 to 15 mmHg) pushes the diaphragm cephalad, so FRC and compliance fall, peak pressures rise and atelectasis and V/Q mismatch develop. CO2 absorption adds hypercarbia and acidosis.
- The carina moves cephalad, so the tube can migrate **endobronchially**.
- Mitigate with a secured tube rechecked after final positioning, lung-protective ventilation (6 to 8 mL/kg, PEEP 5 to 10, recruitment, pressure control) and minute ventilation titrated to ETCO2 and arterial gas.

**Circulation**
- Preload and afterload rise early (central venous shift, neurohumoral response, CO2), then venous return and cardiac output fall as intra-abdominal pressure compresses the IVC. Vagal bradycardia can follow insufflation.
- Mitigate with patient selection, an arterial line, slow insufflation to the lowest working pressure, avoiding hypovolaemia, and treating bradycardia by stopping insufflation and giving atropine.

**Brain and eyes**
- Intracranial and intra-ocular pressure rise, and hypercarbia vasodilates cerebral vessels.
- Mitigate by excluding intracranial pathology and uncontrolled glaucoma, keeping normocapnia, keeping the MAP near baseline, protecting the eyes, and asking the surgeon to return the patient to flat during pauses.

**Face and airway oedema:** perform a cuff leak test before extubation and delay extubation if the leak is absent.

**Positioning:** slipping and brachial plexus or pressure injury (non-slip gel, padded tucked arms, no shoulder braces) and hypothermia.

## Intraoperative considerations for robotic surgery (50%)

- **No access once docked:** the robot covers the head and torso, so secure the airway, lines and limbs before docking, extend the circuit and infusion lines, and rehearse an **emergency undocking drill** so the patient can be made supine and resuscitated quickly.
- **Anaesthetic:** general anaesthesia with a cuffed tube, a **deep neuromuscular block** with quantitative monitoring, because coughing with instruments inside can cause visceral or vascular injury.
- **Monitoring and access:** arterial line, two large cannulae, temperature, and urine output (oliguria is expected, so avoid chasing it with fluid).
- **Complications of insufflation:** endobronchial migration, pneumothorax, surgical emphysema and gas embolism. The Blue Book steps for embolism are to stop insufflation and decompress the abdomen, give 100% oxygen, stop nitrous oxide, support the circulation and consider aspiration through a central line.
- **Team:** agree the plan for conversion to open surgery, redose antibiotics, give VTE prophylaxis and multimodal analgesia.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · Link each physiological effect to a mitigation and address restricted access, team planning and safe emergence.
rubric: Cardiovascular effects of head-down plus pneumoperitoneum, each with a specific mitigation
Respiratory effects (FRC, compliance, atelectasis, CO2) with lung-protective ventilation and gas monitoring
Endobronchial migration and subcutaneous emphysema named, with tube position rechecked
Raised ICP and intra-ocular pressure, with exclusion criteria and MAP near baseline
Face and airway oedema with cuff leak test and delayed extubation
Pressure, nerve and slipping injury, rhabdomyolysis, hypothermia
Robot specific: no access once docked, undocking drill, deep neuromuscular block
Gas embolism steps (stop insufflation, 100% oxygen, stop nitrous oxide) and A to E structure

items.title: 2024.2 Q15: Venous and arterial air embolism
items.q: List the risk factors for venous air embolism and arterial air embolism. (30%) Discuss the diagnosis and management of intraoperative massive venous air embolism in a patient under general anaesthesia. (70%)
items.model:
## Risk factors (30%)

**Venous air embolism** needs an open non-collapsing vein that is above the heart or at sub-atmospheric pressure (Blue Book):
- **Surgical:** operations above heart level (sitting or beach chair, posterior fossa, neck, spine), laparoscopy and hysteroscopy, cell salvage or pressurised infusions, and the myometrium in pregnancy and caesarean section.
- **Vascular access:** insertion or removal of central lines, open or disconnected lines, and gastroscopy.
- **Patient factors:** hypovolaemia, spontaneous inspiration and a head-up position.

**Arterial air embolism** occurs by direct entry (cardiac surgery, bypass, arterial line flushing, pulmonary barotrauma) or **paradoxically** through a PFO or ASD (about a quarter of people have a PFO, from memory) or an intrapulmonary shunt, especially when right-sided pressures rise (PEEP, Valsalva).

## Diagnosis of massive venous air embolism

Slow entry (up to about 10 mL/min) is filtered by the pulmonary capillaries, but rapid entry raises pulmonary artery pressure, reduces left ventricular preload and causes collapse. Under anaesthesia it is detected late and **monitoring is the diagnosis**:
- A sudden **fall in ETCO2**, hypoxia and falling saturation.
- Hypotension, arrhythmia, ST change and a raised CVP.
- A "mill-wheel" murmur, a sudden fall in BIS or cerebral oximetry if there is arterial embolism.
- **Transoesophageal echo** is the gold standard (detects 0.02 mL/kg). Imaging has a high false-negative rate and should not delay treatment.

## Management

- **1.** **Stop further entry:** tell the surgeon, flood the field with saline, lower the site below the heart, release any pneumoperitoneum and stop nitrous oxide, which expands bubbles.
- **2.** **Support:** airway, FiO2 1.0, restore volume and use vasopressors, then inotropes for the failing right ventricle, and start CPR if arrested. Routine head-down (Trendelenburg) positioning is no longer advised; use supine or left lateral decubitus, and do not delay chest compressions to reposition.
- **6.** Consider abandoning or converting the operation if instability recurs. Reserve specialist hyperbaric discussion for suspected arterial embolisation or significant persistent sequelae. Continue oxygen and organ support during transfer.
- **4.** For suspected arterial gas embolism give high-concentration oxygen and discuss urgent hyperbaric treatment with the receiving specialist, even if deficits improve. Continue resuscitation, arrange monitored transfer and avoid delaying for a chamber-specific regimen.

The Blue Book warns of a **biphasic course**, with up to 65% deteriorating a second time, so keep the patient in HDU or ICU.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · Distinguish venous from arterial risk factors. Recognise sudden capnography and circulatory changes and give a clear rescue order.
rubric: Venous risk factors: surgery above the heart, central lines, laparoscopy, hypovolaemia
Arterial risk factors: PFO or ASD, intrapulmonary shunt, direct arterial entry
Diagnosis: falling ETCO2, hypoxia, hypotension, arrhythmia, murmur, TOE
Stop entry: inform surgeon, flood field, release pneumoperitoneum, stop nitrous oxide
FiO2 1.0, vasopressors, right ventricular support and CPR
Aspirate via central line; supine or left lateral instead of routine head-down
Hyperbaric oxygen for arterial embolism, as early as possible
Biphasic course and HDU or ICU admission

items.title: 2024.2 Q12: ERCP for obstructive jaundice from pancreatic cancer
items.q: Discuss the perioperative anaesthetic management considerations of a patient with inoperable pancreatic cancer causing obstructive jaundice who requires endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) intervention.
items.model:
## Preop

**Goals of care:** the cancer is inoperable, so the aim is palliation (relief of jaundice, cholangitis or itch). Agree what the patient wants and what escalation is acceptable.

**Effects of the tumour and the jaundice** (the examiners asked specifically for these):
- **Cachexia and nutrition:** up to 80% of pancreatic cancer patients are cachectic (BJA). Expect hypoalbuminaemia, anaemia, pressure-area risk and low reserve.
- **Jaundice** produces haemodynamic instability, acute kidney injury, myocardial depression, coagulopathy, immunosuppression and poor healing (BJA). Check urea, creatinine, bilirubin, albumin, INR and platelets.
- **Coagulopathy:** vitamin K malabsorption. The Blue Book states the INR does not predict bleeding in liver disease, so do not give plasma for the INR alone; give IV vitamin K and treat bleeding.
- **Cholangitis:** fever, rigors and sepsis need antibiotics before the procedure and an arterial line if unstable.
- **Gastric outlet obstruction** is common with a pancreatic head mass; if present, treat as a full stomach with rapid sequence induction (BJA).
- **Other:** diabetes or new pancreatic diabetes, opioid use for pain (consider a coeliac plexus block later) and cardiorespiratory comorbidity.

## Choice of sedation or general anaesthesia

Both were accepted if justified.
