I favour **general anaesthesia with a cuffed tracheal tube** because the patient is frail, may be septic, has a possible full stomach, lies prone or semi-prone with a shared airway, and the procedure can be long and stimulating. Sedation with anaesthetist-delivered propofol is reasonable for a fit patient with a simple stent exchange, an intact gag and a protected position.

## Intraop

- **Position:** semi-prone or left lateral with a head turn. Induce supine, then turn with a team, pad pressure points and keep the arms out of the fluoroscopy field. Secure the tube, and allow for limited access to the airway.
- **Monitoring:** standard, with capnography, plus an arterial line if septic. Wear lead and use distance and shielding.
- Titrate short-acting agents to physiological reserve and treatment goals. Review renal and hepatic function when selecting adjuncts and reversal. Use quantitative neuromuscular monitoring when blockers are given.

## Postop

Watch for post-ERCP pancreatitis, perforation (surgical emphysema, retroperitoneal air), bleeding after sphincterotomy and ongoing cholangitis. Extubate awake in the lateral position, give simple analgesia and plan HDU if septic.

Assess new abdominal pain, fever or deterioration for post-ERCP pancreatitis, perforation, bleeding or incomplete drainage. In selected patients, rectal NSAID and pancreatic duct stenting can reduce pancreatitis risk. Coordinate prophylaxis with endoscopy and consider renal or bleeding contraindications.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · Address obstructive jaundice, infection, the remote environment, aspiration and choice of sedation or intubation.

items.title: 2023.2 Q8: Perioperative elements that improve emergency laparotomy outcomes
items.q: Discuss the elements of perioperative management that improve outcomes in patients undergoing emergency laparotomy.
items.model:
## Preop

Agree on the urgency with a senior surgeon and anaesthetist. Involve ICU early for shock, organ dysfunction or high predicted mortality. Review imaging promptly to identify ischaemia, perforation, obstruction or a drainable source. Resuscitate and treat sepsis while planning definitive source control. Obtain lactate, renal function, blood count and blood group as appropriate. Use balanced crystalloids and early vasopressor support where indicated, with frequent reassessment. Give appropriate antibiotics promptly for suspected intra-abdominal sepsis. Review antithrombotics, electrolytes, aspiration risk and the need for nasogastric decompression. Decompression does not establish an empty stomach.

Document frailty, baseline function, comorbidities and a validated estimate of operative risk, using the local emergency laparotomy pathway. Scores help communicate risk and plan senior staffing and postoperative destination. Discuss realistically with the patient or surrogate the likely outcomes, alternatives, possible stoma, ICU, treatment ceilings and whether surgery fits their goals. Arrange geriatric input when feasible without delaying time-critical treatment.

## Intraop

Prepare for haemodynamic deterioration during induction. Use a risk-adjusted airway strategy with trained assistance, suction and monitoring. Use direct observation and dynamic assessment to guide fluid, blood and vasopressor treatment instead of chasing a fixed volume or a single urine output. Preserve temperature, oxygen delivery and perfusion. Use lung-protective ventilation with tidal volume based on predicted body weight and individualised PEEP. Provide suitable multimodal analgesia. Shock, coagulopathy and need for neurological or ventilatory monitoring affect regional choices. Coordinate source control, antibiotic redosing, blood-loss response and the decision for definitive versus damage-control surgery.

## Postop

Handover the underlying diagnosis, source-control adequacy, residual contamination, fluid and blood balance, organ support and treatment ceiling. Use planned critical care where needs or risk warrant it. Assess perfusion, respiratory status, renal function and delirium and respond promptly to deviation from expected recovery. Reassess antimicrobial need, provide early nutrition when safe, mobilisation and VTE prophylaxis as appropriate. Involve rehabilitation and geriatric teams when helpful.

ANZELA-QI, NELA and ERAS pathways provide benchmarks and process measures. Audit timing, senior attendance, risk documentation and appropriate critical care, and review complications and mortality. Bundled quality improvement cannot establish that every individual element independently causes a mortality reduction.

A named postoperative lead makes early escalation and handover accountability explicit.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · Examiners wanted links between management and outcomes, including audits, senior input, urgency, imaging, frailty, risk scores and patient wishes.

items.title: 2022.1 Q1: Preoperative optimisation for oesophagectomy
items.q: Describe your preoperative assessment of a patient with oesophageal cancer scheduled for an oesophagectomy and justify your strategy to optimise them before surgery.
items.model:
## Assessment

Oesophagectomy is among the highest-risk elective operations (hospital mortality about 2 to 4%, pulmonary complications 20 to 30%, anastomotic leak about 10%, atrial fibrillation 15 to 20%; all from memory). The examiners wanted risk stratification and optimisation tied to this patient, not generic lists.

**Disease and treatment**
- Type of tumour: squamous (smoking, alcohol) or adenocarcinoma (reflux, obesity).
- **Neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy:** cisplatin (renal, hearing, neuropathy), 5-FU (cardiotoxicity), radiotherapy (pneumonitis, cardiac damage). Check renal function, echocardiography and spirometry afterwards.
- Dysphagia, regurgitation and aspiration risk, weight loss.

**Cardiovascular:** ischaemic disease, heart failure, arrhythmia. Use functional capacity and CPET; an anaerobic threshold under 10 mL/kg/min predicts complications in upper GI surgery (BJA). Echo if there is a murmur, dyspnoea or prior chemotherapy.

**Respiratory:** spirometry and predicted postoperative FEV1 for one-lung ventilation, smoking, COPD, sputum, and aspiration.

**Nutrition and fitness:** weight loss, BMI, albumin and sarcopenia. Screen with MUST or NRS-2002 (Blue Book 2015, BJA), and give 5 to 7 days of nutrition (Blue Book) or high-protein supplements (1.5 g/kg/day, BJA).

**Other:** anaemia, diabetes, alcohol use (withdrawal prophylaxis with benzodiazepines and thiamine, BJA), frailty, and goals of care.

## Risk stratification

Combine ASA grade, age, CPET, spirometry, frailty and surgical factors (approach, access, institutional volume) and discuss risks with the patient, surgeon and ICU.

## Optimisation (justified)

- **Prehabilitation** for 3 to 6 weeks if time allows (BJA ERAS): aerobic and respiratory exercise, inspiratory muscle training and protein.
- **Stop smoking** at least 4 weeks (BJA), treat COPD, and start a bronchodilator and chest physiotherapy plan.
- **Nutrition:** a jejunostomy or enteral feeding if the weight loss is above 15% or the BMI is below 18.5 (BJA ERAS thresholds).
- **Anaemia:** IV iron first line if surgery is within 6 weeks (BJA).
- **Cardiac:** optimise medication, and treat arrhythmia and heart failure.
- **Plan** the analgesia (epidural or paravertebral), one-lung ventilation, postoperative ICU, and ERAS pathway; agree the consent discussion including the possible need for a stoma or conversion.

Review imaging and multidisciplinary staging for resectability and airway or vascular involvement. Assess recent chemotherapy toxicity, swallowing, aspiration and weight loss. Prioritise nutritional intervention where meaningful within the oncological timeline. CPET may support a discussion about risk and recovery when functional capacity is uncertain. Agree ventilation, analgesia and critical care planning with the multidisciplinary team.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · Give a focused preoperative evaluation and justify interventions based on function, nutrition and respiratory reserve.

items.title: 2021.2 Q6: Mitigating risks of prolonged prone surgery
items.q: Discuss the perioperative strategies you would use to mitigate the risks of prolonged surgery in the prone position.
items.model:
## Preop

The examiners expected strategies across the whole perioperative period, not only intraoperative positioning.
- **Selection and consent:** assess cardiorespiratory reserve, BMI, shoulder and neck mobility, and the expected duration and blood loss. Warn the patient about pressure injuries, nerve injury, facial swelling and, above all, **postoperative visual loss**, which is associated with long operations, major blood loss, anaemia, hypotension, and male sex and obesity.
- Optimise anaemia, hypertension and diabetes, and give the team a plan for turning.

## Intraop

- **Airway:** a reinforced, well-secured tube, with the position checked after turning. Keep the head neutral and at or above heart height.
- **Eyes and face:** no pressure on the orbits, use a horseshoe or a foam face support with checks every 15 to 30 minutes, and keep the eyes taped.
- **Respiratory and cardiovascular:** with the abdomen free, intrathoracic compliance and venous return improve and epidural venous pressure falls; a chest or pelvic support that compresses the abdomen does the reverse and reduces venous return. Use an arterial line for long cases, keep the MAP near baseline, avoid anaemia, and use goal-directed fluids.
- **Nerve and pressure injuries:** arms no more than 90 degrees abducted and padded at the elbow (ulnar), no traction on the brachial plexus, padded knees, ankles, genitalia and breasts, and repeated checks.
- **Prolonged surgery:** warm the patient, redose antibiotics at the right interval, use mechanical VTE prophylaxis plus drugs, and watch for rhabdomyolysis and compartment syndrome (BJA principles).
- **Monitoring:** neurophysiological monitoring for spinal surgery needs TIVA and limits muscle relaxants. Plan for emergencies by keeping a trolley ready to turn the patient supine for CPR.

## Postop

Check for facial and airway oedema with a cuff leak test, extubate carefully, assess **vision** early, do a neurological and pressure-area check, give multimodal analgesia, and arrange HDU if there was major blood loss.

For each phase name likely harm and mitigation. Before turning establish the patient’s tolerable neck and limb position, then assign roles and preserve tube, lines and alignment through coordinated movement. During surgery document regular eye checks, airway pressures and perfusion. After return, evaluate oedema and perform a new vision, skin and neurological check. Assess an unexpected visual symptom urgently.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · Give specific strategies across the perioperative course and address access, positioning and monitoring.

items.title: 2021.2 Q4: Venous carbon dioxide embolism in laparoscopy
items.q: Describe the clinical presentation of venous carbon dioxide embolism during laparoscopic surgery and outline your management.
items.model:
## Why CO2 embolism differs from air

The examiners marked down answers that described air embolism. CO2 is about 20 times more soluble than nitrogen, so a small bolus dissolves quickly and is tolerated far better than air. A large bolus can still form a gas lock in the right ventricle and outflow tract and cause collapse, particularly if it enters through a vein at high flow.

**Causes:** the Veress needle or trocar placed in a vein or solid organ, insufflation into a damaged vessel (including parenchymal injury of liver or uterus), high insufflation pressure or flow, and hysteroscopy.

## Clinical presentation

Entry may be sudden or gradual, and detection under anaesthesia depends on monitoring:
- **ETCO2** may rise briefly with absorbed CO2, then fall sharply as dead space increases.
- Falling saturation and pulmonary hypertension, with a rise in CVP and fall in blood pressure.
- Arrhythmia, ST change or bradycardia and asystole.
- A "mill-wheel" murmur, and a sudden fall in BIS or cerebral oximetry if there is paradoxical arterial passage through a PFO (Blue Book).
- **Transoesophageal echocardiography** is the most sensitive monitor (0.02 mL/kg, Blue Book), but you should not wait for it before acting.

## Management

- **1.** **Tell the surgeon immediately and stop insufflation; deflate the pneumoperitoneum** to remove the source.
- **2.** Give **100% oxygen** (FiO2 1.0), stop nitrous oxide, and hyperventilate to increase the CO2 clearance.
- **3.** **Support the circulation:** restore volume, give a vasopressor (noradrenaline or adrenaline) and an RV inotrope, and start CPR with chest compressions if arrested.
- **4.** **Position:** the Blue Book says routine head-down (Trendelenburg) positioning is no longer advised; use supine or left lateral decubitus, and do not delay resuscitation for it.
- **5.** **Aspirate** through an existing central venous catheter, and consider a CVC if one is not in place and the patient is stable enough.
- **6.** Consider abandoning or converting the operation if instability recurs. Reserve specialist hyperbaric discussion for suspected arterial embolisation or significant persistent sequelae. Continue oxygen and organ support during transfer.
- **7.** Keep the patient monitored afterwards because deterioration can be biphasic (up to 65%, Blue Book), and record the event.

**Prevention:** use the agreed safe entry technique, verify insufflation pressure and flow and stop promptly if initial pressures or physiology are unexpected.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · Distinguish CO₂ embolism from air and apply the actual mechanism and rescue priorities to laparoscopy.

items.title: 2019.1 Q5: Haematemesis in alcoholic liver disease needing gastroscopy
items.q: A 61-year-old man presents with a large haematemesis. He has known alcoholic liver disease and sedation is requested for an urgent gastroscopy. Outline your peri-procedural concerns.
items.model:
## Preop

This patient may die from the bleed, so the answer is organised by threat.

**1. Haemorrhage and resuscitation**
- Two large-bore cannulae and an arterial line if unstable. Take bloods including a group and crossmatch, haemoglobin, INR, platelets, fibrinogen, calcium, creatinine, glucose and lactate, with viscoelastic testing.
- **Restrictive transfusion:** haemoglobin target about 70 g/L (80 with cardiovascular disease), because over-transfusion raises portal pressure and rebleeding (Blue Book). Aim for a MAP of about 65 and normal ionised calcium.
- INR alone does not predict bleeding and does not mandate plasma. During ongoing major haemorrhage use the local protocol and laboratory or viscoelastic data to guide haemostatic treatment.

**2. Medical therapy in parallel with endoscopy (the Blue Book bundle)**
- With suspected varices start a vasoactive drug such as octreotide or terlipressin and early antibiotic prophylaxis with local guidance. Consider erythromycin when appropriate. A PPI can be considered while a nonvariceal source remains possible. Reassess after diagnosis.
- Aim for endoscopy within 12 hours after initial resuscitation for suspected varices. Band oesophageal varices. Gastric varices require a subtype-specific endoscopic or radiological plan. Use a covered stent or balloon as an expert bridge in selected uncontrolled bleeding, with airway protection and a definitive rescue plan.

## Intraop

- Sedation is a poor choice if the airway is not protected: blood in the stomach, active haematemesis, encephalopathy, and tense ascites. The Blue Book decides sedation versus general anaesthesia on aspiration risk, airway protection and respiratory reserve, so a large haematemesis favours **general anaesthesia with rapid sequence induction and a cuffed tube**, after resuscitation, with suction and head-up positioning.
- Pre-oxygenate, give a pre-induction vasopressor or bolus, and choose a haemodynamically stable induction at a reduced dose. Use rocuronium with sugammadex, or suxamethonium, with ketamine or etomidate rather than a standard propofol dose.

**4. Alcohol-related and liver-related issues**
- Grade the liver disease (Child-Pugh, MELD), and look for ascites, encephalopathy, hepatorenal syndrome, hepatopulmonary syndrome, and alcoholic cardiomyopathy.
- **Drugs:** reduced doses, prefer fentanyl or remifentanil, cisatracurium or atracurium, avoid pethidine and long-acting benzodiazepines, and limit paracetamol (Blue Book 2017).
- **Withdrawal and thiamine:** give thiamine and benzodiazepine prophylaxis (BJA), watch for delirium tremens, and check magnesium, phosphate and glucose.

## Postop

Extubate after haemostasis and safe recovery of airway protection. Continue the vasoactive and antibiotic course as indicated. Treat encephalopathy if present. Discuss early TIPS eligibility and rescue for rebleeding before leaving the procedure area.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · Recognise chronic liver disease, resuscitation needs, aspiration and the decision about a protected airway, with post-procedure care.

items.title: 2017.2 Q5: Laparoscopic ultra-low colonic resection
items.q: What are the considerations when anaesthetising a patient for a complex laparoscopic ultra-low colonic resection?
items.model:
## Preop

Clarify the indication, duration, anticipated lithotomy and head-down angle, robot if used, vascular or urinary involvement, possible stoma and likelihood of conversion. Assess frailty, nutrition, anaemia, prior pelvic radiotherapy or surgery and cardiorespiratory reserve. Ask whether the patient can tolerate increased airway pressure, hypercarbia and prolonged tilt. Consider renal function, obstructive symptoms and bowel-preparation fluid losses. Consent for analgesia and blood if indicated. Plan VTE prophylaxis, antibiotic timing, stoma counselling and a suitable recovery location. If reserve is limited, discuss an alternative approach early.

## Intraop

Use general anaesthesia with a secured cuffed tube, reliable access and long lines if access will be restricted. Insert an arterial line if supported by comorbidity or expected instability. Pad the arms and legs, protect eyes, avoid excessive hip flexion and secure the patient without excessive shoulder pressure. Confirm lines and tube position again after tilt and insufflation. Agree how to level the patient or undock in an emergency. Review pressure areas and time spent in lithotomy. Severe pain and neurological findings after prolonged lithotomy can signal compartment syndrome.

Pneumoperitoneum and tilt reduce compliance and functional residual capacity. Use predicted-body-weight tidal volumes, individualised PEEP, capnography and an arterial gas if the arterial-to-end-tidal gradient may be wide. Increase minute ventilation as needed, while avoiding excessive pressures and allowing adequate expiration. Use the lowest effective insufflation pressure and limit extreme tilt when possible. Stop insufflation for instability and investigate haemorrhage, vagal bradycardia, embolism or pneumothorax according to timing. Maintain perfusion with balanced crystalloid, appropriately selected boluses and vasopressor support. Avoid fluid overload and sustained hypoperfusion. Use multimodal analgesia or a suitable abdominal wall block, with a contingency for open conversion. Maintain temperature and monitor blood loss.

## Postop

Return to level, reevaluate the airway, ventilation and oedema before extubation and consider delayed extubation after prolonged tilt or physiological instability. Hand over positioning and bleeding risks, effect of conversion, urine output and analgesia. Monitor for leak, stoma or drain losses, ileus, bleeding, AKI, VTE and lower-limb neurovascular complications. Use procedure-appropriate enhanced recovery, oral intake and mobilisation as feasible. A rising lactate with abdominal deterioration requires timely surgical assessment rather than reassurance from an initially smooth recovery.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · The report emphasised the distinctive effects of prolonged surgery, pneumoperitoneum and steep head-down positioning.

items.title: 2017.2 Q3: Positioning for prone spinal surgery in rheumatoid arthritis
items.q: A 55-year-old male with severe steroid-dependent rheumatoid arthritis requires spinal surgery in the prone position. Discuss your considerations for patient positioning for the procedure.
items.model:
## Before turning

Discuss surgical level, need for head fixation, imaging, and acceptable neck position with the spine team. Rheumatoid arthritis can cause atlantoaxial or subaxial instability and cervical myelopathy. Review neurological symptoms, prior imaging and safe movement while awake. Obtain targeted imaging or specialist review when the findings warrant it. Document baseline neurology and joint movement. Temporomandibular restriction or cricoarytenoid involvement can also affect airway planning. Agree an airway technique that limits unwanted cervical movement and maintains oxygenation, including awake intubation when appropriate. Secure and verify the tube before moving. Use a frame that supports chest and pelvis with the abdomen free.

## During transfer and positioning

Appoint a turn leader and allocate specific roles to the airway, neck, limbs and lines. Maintain agreed spinal alignment, move the patient together and minimise traction on fragile joints. Reconfirm ventilation, tube depth, line function and haemodynamics immediately. Position the neck according to the specialist plan and avoid unnecessary extension or rotation. Protect the eyes against direct pressure and confirm they remain clear. Keep shoulders and arms within comfortable range, avoid excessive abduction or elbow extension and pad the ulnar nerves, knees and pressure areas. Protect breasts, genitalia and fragile steroid-exposed skin. Check hand perfusion and avoid compressing monitoring lines. An abdomen left free can reduce venous pressure and facilitate ventilation.

## Maintenance and return to supine

Recheck tube, eyes, supports, pressure areas and limb alignment after draping and surgical movement. Recognise increased airway pressures, hypotension, venous congestion or loss of neuromonitoring signals as reasons to reassess position, oxygen delivery and anaesthetic factors. Manage haemodynamic compromise promptly. In prolonged high-risk spine procedures, address blood loss, hypotension and anaemia as part of reducing visual injury risk. Plan how to turn supine promptly if resuscitation or airway access is needed.

Coordinate the return to supine with the same team and recheck lines, airway and neck alignment. Assess facial or pharyngeal oedema and ensure a safe extubation plan. Perform and document a postoperative neurological and skin check, compare against baseline findings, and urgently assess any weakness, sensory deficit or visual symptom. A perioperative steroid plan is relevant to the patient but cervical protection and positioning remain the focus of this question.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · Address rheumatoid-specific cervical spine protection, and eye, nerve and musculoskeletal injury prevention.

items.title: 2017.1 Q3: Analgesia for open liver resection
items.q: List the methods of analgesia that can be used for patients undergoing open liver resection surgery. (30%) Justify your perioperative pain management strategy. (70%)
items.model:
## Methods of analgesia (30%)

Systemic: paracetamol, NSAIDs, opioids (PCA or infusion), ketamine, lidocaine infusion and gabapentinoids. Regional: **thoracic epidural**, **intrathecal morphine**, continuous **wound infusion** catheters (subcutaneous, subfascial or preperitoneal), **TAP and rectus sheath blocks** or catheters, paravertebral and erector spinae blocks.

## Preop

Review baseline liver function, anticipated extent of resection, renal and bleeding risk, expected incisions and antithrombotic timing. Discuss goals of breathing, coughing and early movement. Thoracic epidural provides effective dynamic analgesia, with risks of sympathectomy, hypotension and catheter removal during evolving coagulopathy. If considering it, agree a coagulation, antithrombotic and removal plan with the acute pain team before insertion. Consider intrathecal morphine in a selected patient with suitable coagulation and capacity for respiratory monitoring, including delayed depression. In an open major resection where postoperative coagulation is expected to change, a surgeon-placed wound catheter or appropriate abdominal wall block can avoid an indwelling neuraxial catheter.

## Intraop

Agree the chosen regional strategy and the dose across teams. I would use an appropriately sited continuous wound infusion or subcostal abdominal wall technique where expertise and incision permit, combined with systemic multimodal analgesia. This addresses somatic wound pain, so provide carefully titrated systemic rescue for visceral discomfort. Calculate total local anaesthetic exposure and account for hepatic handling, body size and concentration. Avoid overlapping an IV lignocaine infusion with other substantial local anaesthetic techniques unless a specific safe institutional protocol supports it. Give adjusted paracetamol when appropriate, considering the size of resection, chronic liver disease, nutritional status and concurrent products. Consider an NSAID only with adequate renal function, haemostasis and surgical agreement. Use short-acting opioid rescue and provide antiemetic prophylaxis.

## Postop

Measure pain at rest and on coughing or movement. Check ventilation and sedation, especially if using neuraxial opioid or PCA. Review renal and hepatic function, haemostasis and catheter function. If epidural analgesia is used, coordinate removal with coagulation trends and antithrombotic timing. Use a named plan for catheter checks, rescue and taper. Support coughing, physiotherapy, mobilisation and oral treatment as recovery permits. Reassess unexpected severe pain for bleeding, bile leak or another surgical complication. Compare techniques by dynamic analgesia, hypotension and ability to mobilise. The best combination depends on incision, physiology and ward monitoring rather than a universal regimen.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · List options first, then justify a specific, safe strategy and the postoperative plan.

items.title: 2016.2 Q1: Pathophysiology of carbon dioxide pneumoperitoneum
items.q: Describe the pathophysiological effects of carbon dioxide pneumoperitoneum during a surgical procedure.
items.model:
## Three separate causes

The effects come from **pressure** (the intra-abdominal pressure of 12 to 15 mmHg), **the gas** (CO2 absorbed across the peritoneum) and **the position** (head-up or head-down), and a good answer keeps them apart.

**Mechanical effects of the pressure**
- The diaphragm is pushed up, so FRC and compliance fall (by about 30 to 50%), peak and plateau pressures rise, and atelectasis and V/Q mismatch develop. Pressures are higher still in obesity, although bariatric patients in reverse Trendelenburg usually stay below 30 cmH2O (BJA).
- At an intra-abdominal pressure above about 10 mmHg the IVC is compressed and venous return falls; above 15 mmHg the splanchnic bed is compressed and cardiac output falls further. Renal blood flow, GFR and urine output fall, and hepatic and splanchnic perfusion fall.
- Pneumoperitoneum has a tamponade effect that reduces venous bleeding during dissection (BJA, hepatic resection), but it also makes CVP unreliable as a measure of volume.

**Effects of absorbed CO2**
- Absorption raises CO2 production by 20 to 30%, producing hypercarbia and respiratory acidosis, usually plateauing after 30 to 60 minutes if ventilation is adjusted. Extraperitoneal insufflation and subcutaneous emphysema increase absorption.
- Hypercarbia causes sympathetic stimulation (tachycardia, hypertension, arrhythmia), cerebral vasodilatation with raised ICP, pulmonary vasoconstriction and a rightward shift of the oxygen curve.

**Reflex and mechanical complications**
- Peritoneal stretch causes a vagal bradycardia or asystole, particularly with rapid insufflation.
- **Gas embolism** (Blue Book 2021: requires an open vein and sub-atmospheric pressure), pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum, endobronchial migration, subcutaneous emphysema, and vascular or visceral injury.

**Effects of position**
Head-up reduces venous return and cardiac output further; head-down raises CVP, ICP and IOP and reduces FRC.

**Other:** hypothermia from cold dry gas, shoulder-tip pain, PONV and venous stasis in the legs with a risk of thrombosis.

**Practical consequence:** the patient with limited cardiac, respiratory or renal reserve tolerates pneumoperitoneum poorly; use low pressure, slow insufflation, monitoring of ETCO2 and airway pressure, and a plan to convert.

The absolute pressure does not predict the same response in every patient. Low venous return, high intrathoracic pressures and head-up positioning may compound hypovolaemia, whereas afterload rises in some patients. A widened arterial-to-end-tidal gradient can make an arterial gas useful in prolonged cases.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · Explain the cardiovascular and respiratory effects and systemic implications of absorbed CO₂.

items.title: 2014.2 Q3: Prolonged steep head-down surgery
items.q: A patient is scheduled to undergo prolonged steep head-down surgery. a. Outline the potential anaesthetic implications of this position in this situation. (50%) b. Describe how you would modify your anaesthetic plan to minimise these. (50%)
items.model:
## a. Anaesthetic implications of prolonged steep head-down position (50%)

**Cardiovascular:** an initial rise in central venous pressure and cardiac preload followed by reduced venous return if there is a pneumoperitoneum, with a risk of raised afterload, arrhythmia, and decompensation in heart failure.

**Respiratory:** the abdominal contents push the diaphragm cephalad, reducing FRC and compliance, causing atelectasis and shunt, and increasing airway pressure. The carina moves up, so the tube can enter the right main bronchus.

**Cerebral and ocular:** venous drainage from the head is impaired, ICP and IOP rise, and perfusion can fall if blood pressure drops. Prolonged cases carry a risk of ischaemic optic neuropathy and corneal abrasion.

**Airway oedema:** conjunctival, facial and laryngeal oedema develop and may cause stridor after extubation.

**Positional injury:** the patient may slide, and brachial plexus, ulnar and common peroneal nerve injuries, pressure injury, compartment syndrome and rhabdomyolysis (with lithotomy) are possible.

**Other:** fluid restriction, oliguria, hypothermia, DVT, and gas embolism or CO2 effects if there is a pneumoperitoneum.

## Preop

Assess cardiorespiratory reserve, raised intracranial pressure, eye disease and aspiration risk. Discuss alternatives or reduced tilt for high-risk patients. Agree working angle, opportunities to reassess and how to return level in an emergency.

## Intraop

a cuffed tracheal tube secured and rechecked at the final position, lung-protective ventilation (6 to 8 mL/kg, PEEP 5 to 10), recruitment manoeuvres, and ETCO2 and blood gas monitoring. Peak pressures above 30 cmH2O need a reason and a response (BJA bariatric: reversible causes first).

**Circulation:** an arterial line for long cases, avoidance of hypovolaemia while avoiding fluid overload, and a vasopressor to keep the MAP near baseline.

**Brain and eyes:** keep the PaCO2 normal, the MAP near baseline and the head neutral, tape and protect the eyes, and consider TIVA when ICP is a concern.

**Positioning:** non-slip gel pads and shoulder supports away from the plexus, padded and tucked arms, avoiding hyperabduction, regular checks, warming and VTE prophylaxis.

## Postop

perform a cuff leak test, return the patient to a level position and wait for the swelling to settle, and keep them in recovery with oximetry and a plan for reintubation.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · Focus on perfusion, ICP and IOP, tube migration, and mitigation appropriate to the individual.

items.title: 2014.1 Q12: Beach chair position for shoulder arthroscopy
items.q: A patient is scheduled on your list for arthroscopic shoulder surgery. The surgery is to be performed in the beach chair position. List the problems associated with this position and describe how you could minimise them.
items.model:
## Problems with the beach chair position

BJA Education describes the position as improving surgical access and reducing venous pressure and bleeding, but with a risk of compromising **haemodynamic and cerebral function**.
- **Hypotension and bradycardia:** venous pooling reduces preload and cardiac output. Up to 20% of patients have a hypotensive or bradycardic event, typically in the sitting position about 30 minutes after an interscalene block. The Bezold-Jarisch reflex is implicated: an underfilled, hypercontractile ventricle stimulates mechanoreceptors, causing sudden loss of sympathetic tone and increased vagal tone (BJA).
- **Cerebral hypoperfusion:** the brain is about 20 to 30 cm above the arm cuff, so the measured pressure overestimates cerebral perfusion pressure (roughly 0.75 mmHg per cm, from memory). This risks cerebral ischaemia, stroke and postoperative visual loss or cognitive injury.
- **Venous air embolism:** the operative site is above the heart (Blue Book 2021).
- **Airway and neck:** tube displacement, neck flexion or rotation with plexus and cord stretch.
- **Interscalene block effects:** phrenic palsy in 25 to 50% even with reduced doses, FEV1 falling up to 40%, Horner's syndrome (about 50%) and recurrent laryngeal nerve block (BJA).
- **Other:** falls, pressure sores, nerve injury (brachial plexus, peroneal), eye injury, and a patient who may slip.

## Minimising the risks

- **Selection and plan:** assess cerebrovascular disease, hypertension and respiratory reserve; discuss awake interscalene block with sedation versus general anaesthesia with or without a block. Avoid interscalene block in patients with limited respiratory reserve; the BJA article suggests prophylactic CPAP or high-flow oxygen and diaphragm ultrasound if used.
- **Positioning:** sit up in stages and not abruptly, secure the head in neutral with a head support, keep the knees slightly flexed with a pillow, and secure the torso and pad pressure points.
- **Monitoring:** measure blood pressure at the level of the brain (transduce an arterial line at the external auditory meatus) or correct for the height difference, and consider cerebral oximetry.
- **Haemodynamics:** avoid preoperative fasting hypovolaemia, give fluids and an early vasopressor (phenylephrine or ephedrine) to keep MAP at or above baseline; treat bradycardia promptly with atropine, with or without a sympathomimetic (BJA).
- **Other:** avoid hypotensive anaesthesia, protect the eyes, secure the tube, and consider a smaller local anaesthetic volume.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · Discuss cerebral hypoperfusion and head, eye, plexus and pressure protection.

items.title: 2014.1 Q9: Laparoscopic right hemicolectomy and pneumoperitoneum
items.q: An otherwise well patient presents for a laparoscopic right hemicolectomy. What are the issues related to the carbon dioxide pneumoperitoneum? How would your intra operative management address these issues?
items.model:
## Issues related to the CO2 pneumoperitoneum

This is an otherwise well patient, so the issues are physiological rather than comorbidity driven:
- **Respiratory:** diaphragm elevation, falling FRC and compliance, higher airway pressures, atelectasis, and **CO2 absorption** causing hypercarbia and acidosis.
- **Cardiovascular:** reduced venous return and cardiac output with rising intra-abdominal pressure, raised afterload and blood pressure, hypercarbic sympathetic effects and arrhythmia. Peritoneal stretch causes **vagal bradycardia** or asystole.
- **Complications:** gas embolism, pneumothorax, subcutaneous emphysema, endobronchial intubation after head-down tilt, vascular or bowel injury.
- **Position:** the operation is done head-down and tilted, with the usual pressure and nerve injury risks.
- **Other:** hypothermia, shoulder-tip pain, PONV, and the need for conversion to open surgery.

## How my intraoperative management addresses them

**Airway and ventilation:** general anaesthesia with a **secured cuffed tube** and muscle relaxation, which gives surgical conditions and prevents coughing. Use volume or pressure control at 6 to 8 mL/kg, PEEP 5 to 10 and recruitment, and raise the minute ventilation (rate rather than large volume) to hold ETCO2 at 4.5 to 5.5 kPa. Peak airway pressures should stay below about 30 cmH2O, with the cause treated if they rise (BJA bariatric).

**Circulation:** monitor ECG, non-invasive pressure and capnography. A modest rise in blood pressure is expected; keep fluids euvolaemic and avoid a large preload deficit before insufflation. Ask the surgeon to insufflate slowly to 12 mmHg, and have atropine drawn up for bradycardia, stopping insufflation if it occurs.

**Embolism and misplacement:** **avoid nitrous oxide**, which expands bowel and any gas embolus (Blue Book), watch the ETCO2 for a sudden fall and check the tube position after tilting.

**Position and temperature:** pad and protect pressure points and nerves, avoid the arm being hyperabducted, use warmed humidified gas and a forced-air warmer, and give VTE prophylaxis.

**Analgesia and recovery:** multimodal analgesia with paracetamol, local anaesthetic at port sites, an opioid and dexamethasone with ondansetron for PONV (a combination if risk is high). Reverse the block fully, and exclude a pneumothorax if unexplained desaturation or high pressures follow.

Reassess ventilation and circulation after insufflation and again after positioning. Abrupt hypotension or a fall in end-tidal CO₂ warrants stopping insufflation while checking ventilation, major bleeding and gas embolism.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · Explain pneumoperitoneum mechanisms and pair each major problem with an intraoperative response.

items.title: 2013.1 Q12: Hazards of the prone position
items.q: What are the hazards of the prone position for patients under general anaesthesia and how can they be minimized?
items.model:
## Hazards of the prone position

**Airway and tube:** accidental extubation or tube displacement during turning, kinking, loss of the airway with no quick access, and facial and airway oedema in long cases that risks obstruction after extubation.

**Respiratory:** with the abdomen free, ventilation-perfusion matching often improves and FRC rises; with a compressed abdomen compliance falls, airway pressure rises and the diaphragm is splinted.

**Cardiovascular:**
- Compression of the IVC reduces venous return and cardiac output and causes hypotension, particularly in obese patients.
- Raised abdominal pressure distends epidural veins and increases bleeding.
- Cardiac arrest is hard to treat: resuscitation requires turning the patient supine, which delays CPR.
- Venous air embolism can occur if the operative site is above the heart.

**Eyes:** corneal abrasion, **central retinal artery occlusion** from orbital pressure, and **ischaemic optic neuropathy** with postoperative visual loss. Risk factors are long surgery, major blood loss, anaemia, hypotension and obesity.

**Nerves:** brachial plexus (arms abducted beyond 90 degrees), ulnar, radial, lateral femoral cutaneous and common peroneal injury. Cervical cord injury from neck rotation or hyperextension.

**Pressure injury and soft tissue:** the face, ears, chest, breasts, iliac crests, genitalia, knees and toes. Rhabdomyolysis and compartment syndrome are possible with long cases.

**Other:** hypothermia and slipping from the supports.

## Minimising the hazards

- **Planning:** select patients (avoid in unstable spine, severe cardiac disease or bad airway where possible), assess the risks and consent for them, and brief the team on turning and the emergency plan.
- **Induction and turning:** induce supine on the trolley, use a reinforced and well-secured tube, turn with at least four people with one person controlling the head and airway, then recheck the tube position, ventilation, the arterial and ECG traces and the lines.
- **Supports:** use frames or bolsters that leave the abdomen free, arms out at less than 90 degrees with the elbows padded, the head neutral on a cushion or Mayfield pins, with the face supported on the forehead and cheeks and the eyes free from pressure. Check every 15 to 30 minutes.
- **Physiology:** use an arterial line in long or high-risk cases, maintain a normal MAP, avoid anaemia and fluid depletion, and warm the patient.
- **Emergency plan:** keep a trolley available and know how to turn the patient supine rapidly for CPR.
- **After surgery:** perform a cuff leak test before extubation, assess vision, nerve and pressure areas early, and give VTE prophylaxis.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · Identify major positional hazards and describe practical measures to reduce them.

items.title: 2012.1 Q2: Beach chair complications and minimisation
items.q: A 65-year-old man is on your list for an arthroscopic acromioplasty that is to be performed in the beachchair position. a. List the complications associated with this position (30%) b. Describe how the risk of these complications can be minimised (70%)
items.model:
## a. Complications of the beach chair position (30%)

- **Haemodynamic:** hypotension and bradycardia from venous pooling (up to 20% of shoulder cases, often about 30 minutes after an interscalene block), through the Bezold-Jarisch reflex in an underfilled, hypercontractile ventricle (BJA).
- **Cerebral:** hypoperfusion, stroke, watershed infarction and cognitive injury, because the brain is above the heart and the measured arm pressure overestimates the cerebral pressure.
- **Embolism:** venous air embolism from surgery above the heart (Blue Book).
- **Eyes:** ischaemic optic neuropathy and postoperative visual loss.
- **Nerve and soft tissue:** brachial plexus stretch, ulnar, peroneal and sciatic injury, and pressure areas.
- **Airway and block:** tube displacement, phrenic palsy (25 to 50%), Horner's syndrome and recurrent laryngeal nerve block if an interscalene block is used.

## b. Minimising the risks (70%)

**Assess and select.** This 65-year-old probably has hypertension and vascular disease. Take a history of stroke, carotid disease, antihypertensive drugs, and respiratory reserve (if an interscalene block is planned). Prepare for general anaesthesia, with or without a block, and discuss risks with the patient.

**Anaesthetic technique.** The interscalene block improves analgesia and reduces opioid use but carries the phrenic palsy risk, so do not use it in a patient with limited respiratory reserve; if used, the BJA article suggests prophylactic CPAP or high-flow oxygen and diaphragm ultrasound. A low dose and a superior trunk block are alternatives. General anaesthesia with a secured cuffed tube is usual for a prolonged procedure.

**Position safely and gradually.** Start with a modest tilt; raise the patient in stages with the legs slightly flexed, secure the head in neutral, and pad the pressure points. Take a baseline blood pressure at each stage.

**Blood pressure and cerebral perfusion.**
- Transduce the arterial line at the level of the external auditory meatus, or correct for the hydrostatic gradient if a cuff is used.
- Maintain the MAP at or above baseline (not just a systolic target), and treat hypotension quickly with phenylephrine or ephedrine and fluid; treat bradycardia with atropine.
- Avoid hypocapnia and deliberate hypotension; consider cerebral oximetry.

**Embolism:** monitor ETCO2, avoid open veins, and manage as in the Blue Book (stop entry, FiO2 1.0, support circulation).

**Eyes and nerves:** protect the eyes, keep the neck neutral, and check the arms and legs.

**Emergence:** return to supine to extubate if cerebral concerns remain, and record the baseline neurological status.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · Weight risk reduction more heavily than listing complications. Address cerebral perfusion, padding and airway access.

items.title: 2010.2 Q3: Alcoholic liver disease and variceal banding
items.q: A 45-year-old man with a longstanding history of alcoholism is booked for upper gastrointestinal endoscopy and banding of oesophageal varices following an episode of haematemesis. (a) How is the severity of this patient's liver disease assessed? (50%) (b) How do these findings influence your evaluation of this patient's perioperative risk? (50%)
items.model:
## a. Assessing the severity of liver disease (50%)

**History and examination:** alcohol intake, previous variceal bleeds, jaundice, encephalopathy, ascites, bleeding tendency, and stigmata of chronic disease (spider naevi, palmar erythema, gynaecomastia, wasting). Look for withdrawal, nutritional state, and hepatic encephalopathy grade.

**Investigations:**
- **Synthetic function:** INR, albumin and bilirubin.
- **Haematology:** platelets (hypersplenism), haemoglobin and viscoelastic tests.
- **Renal and electrolytes:** urea, creatinine, sodium, potassium; magnesium and phosphate in alcohol use.
- **Imaging and endoscopy:** ultrasound or CT for ascites, splenomegaly, portal vein; gastroscopy for varices.
- **Portal hypertension:** HVPG of 6 mmHg or more is portal hypertension and over 10 is clinically significant (Blue Book 2023).
- **Cardiopulmonary:** ECG, echocardiography for alcoholic cardiomyopathy and pulmonary pressures, and blood gases.

**Scoring:**
- **Child-Pugh** (bilirubin, albumin, INR, ascites, encephalopathy) classes A, B, C.
- **MELD** (bilirubin, INR, creatinine, sodium in newer versions) and the change in MELD over time.

## b. Influence on perioperative risk (50%)

Estimate risk using severity, prior decompensation and the proposed operation. Child–Pugh and MELD aid staging. Add a surgery-specific estimate such as VOCAL-Penn when applicable. Discuss ascites control, frailty, elective timing and alternatives with hepatology and surgery. A single score does not define operability.

**How the findings change management:**
- **Endoscopic banding is urgent, so it goes ahead** after resuscitation, but a Child C patient needs ICU backup, a secured airway and a discussion about goals.
- **Ascites:** reduced FRC and aspiration risk; use rapid sequence induction and consider paracentesis.
- **Coagulopathy:** the INR does not predict bleeding, so do not give plasma for the INR alone; use viscoelastic testing.
- **Cardiovascular:** hyperdynamic circulation, low SVR, alcoholic cardiomyopathy.
- Investigate unexplained hypoxaemia or exertional symptoms for hepatopulmonary syndrome and portopulmonary hypertension. Echocardiography screens for pulmonary hypertension, with specialist-directed right-heart catheterisation to establish the diagnosis.
- **Renal:** hepatorenal syndrome risk; avoid hypovolaemia and nephrotoxins.
- **Drugs:** reduced doses, avoid pethidine, and use fentanyl or remifentanil and cisatracurium or atracurium.
- **Alcohol:** withdrawal prophylaxis and thiamine.
- **Disposition:** HDU after surgery.

Add procedure-specific risk and urgency to MELD or Child–Pugh estimates. Assess prior decompensation, renal function, nutrition and cardiopulmonary reserve. Use these findings to plan monitoring, drug titration and the likelihood of needing ICU. Urgent haemostasis changes the balance of delaying versus proceeding. Discuss vasopressors and blood access for ongoing bleeding.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · Assess liver severity clinically and with investigations, then connect severity to the risk of this particular procedure.

items.title: 2010.1 Q3: BMI 48 for diagnostic laparoscopy
items.q: A 20 year old female with a body mass index of 48 kg/m² presents for an elective diagnostic laparoscopy for endometriosis. She has no other medical conditions. Describe the potential problems associated with anaesthetising this patient.
items.model:
## Preop

Clarify body habitus and positioning needs, exercise tolerance, symptoms of OSA or hypoventilation, reflux, past anaesthetic history and medication exposure. Absence of known comorbidity does not exclude OSA. Check mask ventilation and intubation predictors. Plan an appropriate table, transfer aids, correctly sized blood-pressure cuff, access and ultrasound if needed. Discuss expected tilt and working pressure with the surgeon. Confirm indication for and feasibility of day discharge. Assess VTE risk and agree suitable mechanical measures and medication when indicated.

## Intraop

Reduced functional residual capacity and higher oxygen consumption shorten the safe apnoea time. Use a head-up ramp, preoxygenate with a good mask seal and use apnoeic oxygenation as appropriate. Use first-line videolaryngoscopy in line with current obesity-airway guidance, with a clear oxygenation rescue plan. Choose rapid-sequence precautions by aspiration risk rather than BMI alone. Use drug-specific weight scalars and titration, and quantitative neuromuscular monitoring. Position limbs securely and review pressure areas and line function after tilt.

Pneumoperitoneum and head-down tilt worsen compliance and ventilation-perfusion matching and increase CO₂ load. Use tidal volume based on predicted body weight, individualised PEEP and sufficient minute ventilation. Reassess plateau pressures, end-tidal CO₂ and haemodynamics after insufflation. Ask for a lower working pressure or reduced tilt if physiology deteriorates. Exclude endobronchial tube migration or pneumothorax if airway pressures rise abruptly. Use haemodynamic assessment to guide fluid or vasopressor therapy, and stop insufflation if sudden bradycardia or instability suggests a relationship. Give multimodal analgesia with paracetamol, an NSAID if suitable and port-site infiltration. Individualise antiemetic prophylaxis.

## Postop

Plan awake, head-up extubation with adequate quantitative reversal and oxygenation. Observe for obstruction, hypoventilation and recurrent desaturation, particularly if opioids are needed. Use CPAP or NIV where indicated and increase monitoring if events recur. Encourage early mobilisation and implement the VTE plan. For discharge check stable respiratory function, tolerable pain and nausea, escort and support. Preserve scope by judging likely issues proportionately. In an otherwise healthy young patient a short procedure can often proceed with careful preparation, monitoring and appropriate recovery without routinely adding invasive lines or ICU admission.

Recheck patient positioning, respiratory mechanics and adequacy of analgesia before transfer.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · The report prioritised monitoring, equipment, airway, ventilation, pharmacology, pneumoperitoneum, analgesia and postoperative respiratory/VTE risk.

items.title: 2009.1 Q6: Physiological effects of CO₂ pneumoperitoneum
items.q: Describe the physiological effects of pneumoperitoneum with CO2 for laparoscopic surgery.
items.model:
## Effects of the raised intra-abdominal pressure

**Respiratory**
- The diaphragm moves up, so FRC and lung compliance fall, airway pressures rise and atelectasis and V/Q mismatch develop.
- The tidal volume must be monitored, because pressure-controlled ventilation may deliver less volume.

**Cardiovascular**
- Venous return: IVC compression reduces preload at pressures above about 10 mmHg; above about 15 mmHg cardiac output falls further.
- Afterload and blood pressure rise from direct aortic compression and neurohumoral release (catecholamines, vasopressin, renin-angiotensin).
- The net effect is a lower cardiac output with a higher SVR and MAP, which is poorly tolerated in heart failure or hypovolaemia.
- Peritoneal stretch causes vagal bradycardia, sometimes asystole.

**Renal and splanchnic:** reduced renal blood flow, GFR and urine output (typically reversible), and reduced hepatic and bowel perfusion.

**Neurological:** raised ICP from a combination of hypercarbia and raised intrathoracic pressure that impairs venous drainage.

## Effects of CO2 absorption

- CO2 crosses the peritoneum, increasing CO2 elimination requirements by around 20 to 30%. Hypercarbia and respiratory acidosis develop unless the minute ventilation is raised, and levels often plateau after 30 to 60 minutes.
- Hypercarbia increases sympathetic tone (tachycardia, hypertension, arrhythmia), dilates cerebral vessels, and increases pulmonary vascular resistance.
- Absorption is greater with extraperitoneal gas or subcutaneous emphysema.

## Effects of position

Head-up (for upper abdominal surgery) lowers venous return and blood pressure; head-down (for pelvic surgery) raises CVP, ICP, IOP and airway pressure.

## Complications

Gas embolism (requires an open vein with sub-atmospheric pressure, Blue Book 2021), pneumothorax and pneumomediastinum, subcutaneous emphysema, endobronchial migration, vascular or visceral injury, regurgitation, hypothermia, and shoulder-tip pain and PONV afterwards.

## Pulling it together

The important clinical point is that healthy patients tolerate this well, but those with cardiac, respiratory or renal disease do not, and the surgeon must insufflate slowly, keep the pressure low and be ready to deflate or convert. BJA Education also notes that the pneumoperitoneum has a tamponade effect that reduces venous bleeding but makes the CVP unreliable.

Mechanisms are additive and vary by patient, insufflation pressure and posture. Diagnose perfusion changes by timing and physiology. A sudden decline in end-tidal CO₂ is different from the gradual rise expected with absorption and warrants assessment for low cardiac output, major bleeding, embolism or a ventilation problem.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · Cover circulatory, respiratory, metabolic and other effects of raised pressure, absorbed gas and position.

items.title: 2008.2 Q3: Suspecting and managing venous gas embolism
items.q: What would make you suspect venous gas embolism occurring during a surgical procedure? Briefly outline the principles of management of venous gas embolism causing haemodynamic compromise.
items.model:
## Recognition

Suspect venous gas embolism when gas can enter open veins or is delivered under pressure. Examples include laparoscopic insufflation, liver surgery with exposed veins, sitting neurosurgery and catheter insertion, removal or unprimed pressurised infusions. Ask what happened immediately before instability. A sudden fall in end-tidal CO₂, with hypotension or tachyarrhythmia, can reflect loss of pulmonary perfusion from gas in the right ventricle or pulmonary circulation. Hypoxaemia, increased right-sided pressure, acute right ventricular dysfunction and cardiac arrest may follow. A mill-wheel murmur is insensitive and should not delay action. During laparoscopy CO₂ embolism can cause a transient early rise in end-tidal CO₂, then a fall with substantial obstruction. Consider paradoxical or arterial embolisation if focal neurological findings or myocardial ischaemia develop.

Check the airway, circuit, ventilation and arterial waveform in parallel. Major haemorrhage, thrombotic pulmonary embolism, tension pneumothorax, anaphylaxis and severe low output can mimic the findings. Use available focused echocardiography to assess gas and right heart function when it will not delay resuscitation. A negative study after transient embolisation does not exclude the diagnosis.

## Management

Call for help, inform the surgeon and prevent further entry. Stop insufflation and release pneumoperitoneum in the relevant case. Flood or cover an open venous field and achieve surgical control, or clamp and secure a suspected intravenous source. Give 100% oxygen, discontinue nitrous oxide, secure ventilation and restore perfusion with appropriate fluid and vasopressors. Initiate standard resuscitation promptly if pulseless. Chest compressions support flow and may help relieve right-heart gas obstruction. Consider aspiration through a correctly positioned central line if already present and practical, without delaying source control or CPR. Position manoeuvres have limited evidence and must not interfere with definitive rescue.

## After stabilisation

Reassess haemodynamics, blood gases and the neurological state, including the possibility of arterial embolism. Provide monitored or intensive care observation as indicated. Discuss urgent hyperbaric oxygen referral for suspected arterial cerebral gas embolism or persistent major neurological findings while continuing high-concentration oxygen and stabilisation. Evaluate the mechanism with the surgical team before contemplating re-insufflation or restarting a procedure. Document timing, response and prevention measures.

Record any suspected arterial involvement for urgent neurological and hyperbaric assessment.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · The report expected entry mechanisms, signs and an effective rescue sequence. End-tidal CO₂ fall, echo and timing are especially useful.

items.title: 2007.2 Q5: Beach chair position for shoulder arthroscopy in a 110 kg patient
items.q: A 50 year old, 110kg builder is on your list for an arthroscopic acromioplasty which is to be performed in the beach chair position. List the problems associated with this position and describe how you could minimise them.
items.model:
## Problems in a 110 kg builder

The question names a heavy, manual-working man, so apply the beach chair problems to his specifics.

**Haemodynamic and cerebral**
- Hypotension and bradycardia from venous pooling, including the Bezold-Jarisch reflex (up to 20% of cases, typically about 30 minutes after an interscalene block, BJA).
- Cerebral hypoperfusion: the brain is above the arm cuff, so the measured pressure overestimates the cerebral perfusion pressure. A builder is likely to be hypertensive and a smoker, so he is more likely to have cerebrovascular disease and to depend on a higher pressure.
- Venous air embolism: the operative site is above the heart (Blue Book).

**Respiratory and airway**
- Obesity: reduced FRC, rapid desaturation and a possibly difficult airway; the BJA bariatric article advises a ramped position and preoxygenation with end-tidal oxygen of 90%.
- Sleep apnoea risk: screen with STOP-Bang.
- Interscalene block causes phrenic palsy in 25 to 50% even with low doses and reduces FEV1 by up to 40%, which obese patients tolerate poorly (BJA).

**Other:** manual-handling risk for staff and for the patient (slipping from the chair), nerve injury (brachial plexus, peroneal), pressure areas, and the eyes.

## Minimising the risks

- **Assessment:** record the blood pressure and any cerebrovascular, cardiac, respiratory or sleep apnoea history. Discuss the options.
- **Equipment:** check the beach chair rating for 110 kg, and have enough staff and a hover mattress for transfer.
- **Technique:** general anaesthesia with a secured tracheal tube is the safe choice, since the airway is not accessible; if an interscalene block is wanted, use a low dose or a superior trunk block and prepare for phrenic palsy (CPAP or high-flow oxygen, diaphragm ultrasound).
- **Dosing:** dose drugs by weight scalar: lean weight for propofol induction, rocuronium and fentanyl, and adjusted weight for infusions and sugammadex (BJA bariatric).
- **Position and pressure:** ramp for induction, then sit up in stages with the head neutral, the knees slightly flexed and the pressure points padded.
- **Blood pressure:** transduce at the level of the brain, keep the MAP at or above baseline, and treat hypotension rapidly with a vasopressor, atropine for bradycardia.
- **Embolism:** monitor ETCO2 and manage per the Blue Book if it occurs.
- **Recovery:** extubate when awake and upright, give multimodal analgesia, and watch the respiratory pattern.
